texts.label: text
texts.orig: For more than 50 years, ISACA® (www. isaca.org) has advanced the best talent, expertise and learning in technology. ISACA equips individuals with knowledge, credentials, education and community to progress their careers and transform their organizations, and enables enterprises to train and build quality teams. Among those credentials, ISACA advances and validates business-critical skills and knowledge through the globally respected Certified Information Systems Auditor® (CISA®), Certified in Risk and Information Systems Control® (CRISC®), Certified Information Security Manager® (CISM®), Certified in the Governance of Enterprise IT® (CGEIT®) and Cera  rd       (     and learning organization that leverages the expertise of its 145,000 members who work in information security, governance, assurance, risk and privacy to drive innovation through technology. It has a presence in 188 countries, including more than 220 chapters worldwide.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: ISACA is pleased to offer the sixteenth edition of the CISM® Review Manual. The purpose of the manual is to provide CISM candidates with information and references to assist in the preparation and study for the Certified Information Security Manager® (CISM) exam.
texts.text: ISACA is pleased to offer the sixteenth edition of the CISM® Review Manual. The purpose of the manual is to provide CISM candidates with information and references to assist in the preparation and study for the Certified Information Security Manager® (CISM) exam.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The CISM® Review Manual is updated regularly to keep pace with rapid changes in the management of information security. As with previous manuals, the sixteenth edition is the result of contributions from many qualified authorities who have generously volunteered their time and expertise. We respect and appreciate their contributions and hope their efforts provide extensive educational value to CISM manual readers.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The sample questions contained in this manual are designed to depict the types of questions typically found on the CISM exam and to give further clarity to the content presented in this manual. The CISM exam is a practice-based exam. Simply reading the reference material in this manual will not properly prepare candidates for the exam. The self-assessment questions are included for guidance only. Scoring results do not indicate future individual exam success.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An international job practice analysis is conducted periodically to maintain the validity of the CISM certification program. A new job practice forms the basis of the CISM exam beginning in 2022.
texts.text: An international job practice analysis is conducted periodically to maintain the validity of the CISM certification program. A new job practice forms the basis of the CISM exam beginning in 2022.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The primary focus areas of the job practice are the current tasks performed and the knowledge used by CISMs. By gathering evidence of the current work practice of CISMs, ISACA ensures that the CISM program continues to meet the high standards set for the certification of professionals throughout the world.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Overview
texts.text: Overview

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The CISM® Review Manual 16th Edition is a reference guide designed to assist candidates in preparing for the CISM examination. The manual is one source of preparation for the exam but should not be thought of as the only source or viewed as a comprehensive collection of all the information and experience required to pass the exam. No single publication offers such coverage and detail.
texts.text: The CISM® Review Manual 16th Edition is a reference guide designed to assist candidates in preparing for the CISM examination. The manual is one source of preparation for the exam but should not be thought of as the only source or viewed as a comprehensive collection of all the information and experience required to pass the exam. No single publication offers such coverage and detail.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As candidates read the manual and encounter topics that are new to them or ones in which they feel their knowledge and experience are limited, additional references should be sought. The examination will be composed of questions testing the candidate's technical and practical knowledge, and ability to apply the knowledge (based on experience) in given situations.

texts.orig: Preparing for the CISM Exam
texts.text: Preparing for the CISM Exam

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The CISM exam evaluates a candidate's practical knowledge based on experiences and application of the job practice domains as described in this review manual. We recommend that the candidate look to multiple resources to prepare for the exam, including this review manual and external publications. This section includes some tips for studying for the exam.

We recommend that the candidate look to multiple resources to prepare for the exam, including this review manual and external publications. This section includes some tips for studying for the exam.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Actual exam questions test the candidate's practical application of relevant knowledge. At the end of each chapter, a sample self-assessment, consisting of questions, answers and explanations, introduces the question structure and general content. Remember that the sample questions may not be similar to questions appearing on the actual exam. Use reference material to find other publications that offer more detailed information on the topics addressed in this manual.

texts.label: text

texts.orig: Types of Questions on the CISM Exam
texts.text: Types of Questions on the CISM Exam

texts.label: text
texts.orig: CISM exam questions are developed with the intent of measuring and testing practical knowledge and the application of information security management principles. All questions are presented in a multiplechoice format and are designed to elicit one best answer.
texts.text: CISM exam questions are developed with the intent of measuring and testing practical knowledge and the application of information security management principles. All questions are presented in a multiplechoice format and are designed to elicit one best answer.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The candidate is cautioned to read each question carefully. Knowing that these types of questions are asked will go a long way toward answering them correctly. The best answer is one of the choices provided. There can be many potential solutions to the problems posed in the scenarios, depending on industry, geographical location, etc. It is advisable to consider the information provided in the question and to determine the best answer among the options provided.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Each CISM question has a stem (question) and four options (answer choices). The candidate is asked to choose the correct or best answer from the options. The stem may be in the form of a question or incomplete statement. In some instances, a scenario or description may be included. These questions normally describe a situation and require the candidate to answer two or more questions based on the information provided.

texts.orig: 1. A. Policies have to be developed to support the security strategy, and an architecture can only be developed after policies are completed (i.e., the security strategy is not the basis for architecture— policies are).
texts.text: A. Policies have to be developed to support the security strategy, and an architecture can only be developed after policies are completed (i.e., the security strategy is not the basis for architecture— policies are).

texts.text: A. Effective communication may assist in making information security more palatable, but that is not the most important aspect.

texts.orig: 3. A. Corporate counsel is generally involved primarily with stock issues and the associated filings required by regulators and with contract matters. It is unlikely that legal staff will be current on information security regulations and legal requirements.
texts.text: A. Corporate counsel is generally involved primarily with stock issues and the associated filings required by regulators and with contract matters. It is unlikely that legal staff will be current on information security regulations and legal requirements.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. While it can be useful to stay abreast of all current and emerging regulations, it is, as a practical matter, nearly impossible—especially for a multinational company.
texts.text: While it can be useful to stay abreast of all current and emerging regulations, it is, as a practical matter, nearly impossible—especially for a multinational company.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. Because departments such as human resources, finance and legal are most often subject to new regulations and must be involved in determining how best to meet the existing and emerging requirements, they typically would be most aware of these regulations. Treating regulations as another risk puts them in the proper perspective, and the mechanisms to deal with them should already exist. The fact that there are so many regulations makes it unlikely that they can all be specifically addressed efficiently. Many do not currently have significant consequences and may be addressed by compliance with other regulations. The most relevant response to regulatory requirements is to determine potential impact to the enterprise, just as with any other risk.

texts.orig: Part A: Enterprise Governance
texts.text: Part A: Enterprise Governance

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information can be defined as "data endowed with meaning and purpose." Information plays a critical role in all aspects of our lives. Information has become an indispensable component of conducting business for virtually all enterprises. In a growing number of companies, information is the business. Similarly, a broad array of technology continues to make it possible to access information. Together, IT constitutes key elements in every enterprise.
texts.text: Information can be defined as "data endowed with meaning and purpose." Information plays a critical role in all aspects of our lives. Information has become an indispensable component of conducting business for virtually all enterprises. In a growing number of companies, information is the business. Similarly, a broad array of technology continues to make it possible to access information. Together, IT constitutes key elements in every enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Enterprise IT is increasingly important. Because a majority of national critical infrastructures in the developed world are controlled by the private sector, much of the task of protecting critical information ręsources falls squarely on private corporations. In many enterprises, reponsibility for that resource protection resides within two important and distinct components— governance and management. COBIT describes them as follows:
texts.text: Enterprise IT is increasingly important. Because a majority of national critical infrastructures in the developed world are controlled by the private sector, much of the task of protecting critical information ręsources falls squarely on private corporations. In many enterprises, reponsibility for that resource protection resides within two important and distinct components— governance and management. COBIT describes them as follows:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Governance ensures that the needs of various stakeholders are evaluated to determine balanced, agreed-on enterprise objectives. Those objectives are then used to set direction (through prioritization and decision making) and to monitor performance and compliance.
texts.text: Governance ensures that the needs of various stakeholders are evaluated to determine balanced, agreed-on enterprise objectives. Those objectives are then used to set direction (through prioritization and decision making) and to monitor performance and compliance.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Management plans, builds, runs and monitors activities, in alignment with the direction set by the governance body, to achieve enterprise objectives.
texts.text: Management plans, builds, runs and monitors activities, in alignment with the direction set by the governance body, to achieve enterprise objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Given the criticality of IT, one would expect those factors to be key considerations for the governing body. However, studies show a large percentage of enterprises do not adequately address either existing or emerging security issues. Some enterprise leaders continue to believe that existing information security programs are insufficient to meet the needs of the enterprise and often feel that the security budget is inadequate to address current risk effectively.
texts.text: Given the criticality of IT, one would expect those factors to be key considerations for the governing body. However, studies show a large percentage of enterprises do not adequately address either existing or emerging security issues. Some enterprise leaders continue to believe that existing information security programs are insufficient to meet the needs of the enterprise and often feel that the security budget is inadequate to address current risk effectively.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security failures can be seen predominantly as a failure of governance and cannot be solved by technology alone. The need for adequate protection of information resources needs to be raised at the board level, like other critical governance functions, to lead to action. The complexity, relevance and criticality of information security and its governance mandate that it be addressed and supported at the highest organizational levels. Similarly, governance objectives increasingly include the need to determine the internal and external requirements for the enterprise's privacy programs and practices. While these objectives are distinct from information security considerations and are the jurisdiction of a data privacy engineer,' the governance body should ensure that both security and privacy are adequately addressed throughout the enterprise.

The need for adequate protection of information resources needs to be raised at the board level, like other critical governance functions, to lead to action. The complexity, relevance and criticality of information security and its governance mandate that it be addressed and supported at the highest organizational levels. Similarly, governance objectives increasingly include the need to determine the internal and external requirements for the enterprise's privacy programs and practices. While these objectives are distinct from information security considerations and are the jurisdiction of a data privacy engineer,' the governance body should ensure that both security and privacy are adequately addressed throughout the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ultimately, to achieve significant improvement in information security, senior management and the board of directors must be held accountable for information security governance and must provide the necessary leadership, organizational structures, oversight, resources and processes to ensure that information security governance is an integral and transparent part of enterprise governance. Because information security risk is a business risk and has direct line of sight to business objectives in most enterprises, accountability among security practitioners and business leaders regarding enterprise risk decisions needs to be balanced.
texts.text: Ultimately, to achieve significant improvement in information security, senior management and the board of directors must be held accountable for information security governance and must provide the necessary leadership, organizational structures, oversight, resources and processes to ensure that information security governance is an integral and transparent part of enterprise governance. Because information security risk is a business risk and has direct line of sight to business objectives in most enterprises, accountability among security practitioners and business leaders regarding enterprise risk decisions needs to be balanced.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Increasingly, those who understand the scope and depth of risk to information take the position that information, as a critical resource, must be treated with the same care, caution and prudence as any other asset essential to the survival of the enterprise.
texts.text: Increasingly, those who understand the scope and depth of risk to information take the position that information, as a critical resource, must be treated with the same care, caution and prudence as any other asset essential to the survival of the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Often, the focus of protection has been on the IT systems that process and store the vast majority of information rather than on the information itself. However, this approach is too narrow to accomplish the level of integration, process assurance and overall security that are required. Information security takes the larger view that content and information, and knowledge based on it, must be adequately protected, regardless of how it is handled, processed, transported or stored. Increasingly, this protection includes the need to consider cloud-based technology and other virtual technology platforms.
texts.text: Often, the focus of protection has been on the IT systems that process and store the vast majority of information rather than on the information itself. However, this approach is too narrow to accomplish the level of integration, process assurance and overall security that are required. Information security takes the larger view that content and information, and knowledge based on it, must be adequately protected, regardless of how it is handled, processed, transported or stored. Increasingly, this protection includes the need to consider cloud-based technology and other virtual technology platforms.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Enterprises exist to create value for their stakeholders. Consequently, any enterprise—commercial or not—has value creation as a governance objective. Value creation means realizing benefits at an optimal resource cost while optimizing risk (figure 1.1). Benefits can take many forms, such as financial for commercial enterprises and high-quality public service for government entities.

texts.orig: Senior management is increasingly confronted by the need to stay competitive in the global economy and heed the promise of ever greater gains from the deployment of more information resources. Even as enterprises reap those gains, the increasing dependence on information and the systems that support it, and the advancing risk from an increasing host of threats, are forcing management to make difficult and often costly decisions about how to effectively address information security. In addition, scores of new and existing laws and regulations are increasingly demanding compliance and higher levels of accountability due to government efforts to address increasingly sophisticated attacks and growing losses that pose mounting threats to their national critical infrastructures.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security governance includes the elements required to provide senior management assurance that its direction and intent are reflected in the security posture of the enterprise. This is achieved by using a structured approach to implementing a security program. Once the elements are in place, senior management can be confident that adequate and effective information security will protect the enterprise's vital information assets.

texts.text: 1.1.2 Scope and Charter of Information Security Governance

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security deals with all aspects of information in any medium (e.g., written, spoken, electronic), regardless of whether it is being created, viewed, transported, stored or destroyed. It differs from IT security, which is concerned with security of information within the boundaries of the technology domain, usually in a custodial capacity. It is important to note this distinction. IT usually is not the owner of most of the information in its systems; rather, it owns the machinery that processes it. The information is in IT's care, control and custody, and IT functions as a custodian for the data owners.

texts.orig: 1.2 Organizational Culture
texts.text: 1.2 Organizational Culture

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security is primarily influenced through transparency and accountability throughout the enterprise culture. Culture is represented by organizational behavior, methods for navigating and influencing the enterprise's formal and informal structures to get work done, attitudes, norms, level of teamwork, existence or lack of turf issues, and geographic dispersion. Culture is impacted by individual backgrounds, work ethics, values, experiences, filters or blind spots, and the perceptions of life that individuals bring to the workplace. Every enterprise has a culture, whether it was purposely designed or simply emerged over time as a reflection of the leadership, and it must be considered in determining roles and responsibilities.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security primarily involves logical and analytical activities. However, building relationships, fostering teamwork and influencing organizational attitudes toward a positive security culture rely more on good interpersonal skills. The astute information security program manager will recognize the importance of developing both types of skills as essential to being an effective manager.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Building a security-aware culture depends on individuals in their respective roles performing their jobs in a way that protects information assets. All individuals, no matter what their level or role within the enterprise, should be able to articulate how information security relates to their role. For this to happen, the security manager must plan communications, participate in committees and projects, and provide individual attention to end users' and managers' needs. The security department should be able to answer the questions "What is in it for me?" and "Why should I care?" for every person in the enterprise. Once these questions have been answered, effective communications can be tailored to support the appropriate messages.

texts.orig: 1.2.1 General Rules of Use/Acceptable Use Policy
texts.text: 1.2.1 General Rules of Use/Acceptable Use Policy

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To support a risk-aware and secure enterprise culture, all participants need to understand what behavior is acceptable, what activities are required and what actions are explicitly prohibited. An acceptable use policy provides a user-friendly summary of what personnel should do and avoid doing. This policy can detail—in everyday terms and in a straightforward, concise manner—the obligations and responsibilities of all users. It is necessary to effectively communicate the acceptable use policy to all users and ensure it is read and understood. The use policy should be provided to all new personnel who will have access to information assets, regardless of employment status.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Typically, the rules of use for all personnel include the policy and standards for access control, classification, marking and handling of documents and information, reporting requirements disclosure constraints, mobile computing, unlawful uses and enforcement. They may also include rules on email and Internet usage. The rules of use provide a general security baseline for the entire enterprise. It is often necessary to provide supplemental or additional information to specific groups in the enterprise, consistent with their responsibilities.

texts.orig: 1.2.2 Ethics
texts.text: 1.2.2 Ethics

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Many enterprises have implemented ethics training to provide guidance on what the enterprise considers legal and appropriate behavior. This approach is most common when individuals are required to engage in activities of a particularly sensitive nature such as monitoring user activities, penetration testing, and accessing sensitive personal data. Information security personnel must be sensitive to potential conflicts of interest or activities that may be perceived as detrimental to the enterprise. Objectives and activities for ethical behavior should be coordinated with objectives and activities for privacy and data protection to ensure consistent and comprehensive consideration. These activities might include integration of data ethics frameworks² that can help define processes for appropriate and responsible data use in the enterprise.

These activities might include integration of data ethics frameworks² that can help define processes for appropriate and responsible data use in the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security managers can set an example by sharing and adhering to their own ethical standards. The ISACA Code of Professional Ethics³ is one example that guides the professional and personal conduct of members of the association and its certification holders. All information security personnel should refer to and acknowledge the enterprise's code of conduct or similar organizational policy for guidance on how to identify and report potential conflicts of interest. Examples of conflicts of interest include but are not limited to selfdealing, accepting gifts, improper influence, dual/multiple employment and use of corporate assets for private advantage. The signed acceptance of the code should be kept as a part of employee records.

texts.orig: 1.3 Legal, Regulatory and Contractual Requirements
texts.text: 1.3 Legal, Regulatory and Contractual Requirements

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Each enterprise faces a broad array of requirements derived from local and international laws, other regulatory oversight mandates and contract-specific provisions related to information security. In preparation for creating strategy, the information security manager must gather as much information as possible about these overarching requirements. Information security is inevitably intertwined with questions of privacy; intellectual property; and contractual, civil and criminal law. Any effort to design and implement an effective information security strategy must be built on a solid understanding of the pertinent legal requirements and restrictions.
texts.text: Each enterprise faces a broad array of requirements derived from local and international laws, other regulatory oversight mandates and contract-specific provisions related to information security. In preparation for creating strategy, the information security manager must gather as much information as possible about these overarching requirements. Information security is inevitably intertwined with questions of privacy; intellectual property; and contractual, civil and criminal law. Any effort to design and implement an effective information security strategy must be built on a solid understanding of the pertinent legal requirements and restrictions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Different regions in a global enterprise may be governed by conflicting laws. For example, the level of legislative focus on privacy differs in different parts of the world, resulting in stricter privacy laws and regulations in some jurisdictions. In some countries, thorough background checks may be performed on new employees—checks that are illegal in other countries. To address these situations, the global enterprise may need to establish different security strategies for each regional division, or it can base policy on the most restrictive requirements to be consistent across the enterprise.

For example, the level of legislative focus on privacy differs in different parts of the world, resulting in stricter privacy laws and regulations in some jurisdictions. In some countries, thorough background checks may be performed on new employees—checks that are illegal in other countries. To address these situations, the global enterprise may need to establish different security strategies for each regional division, or it can base policy on the most restrictive requirements to be consistent across the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A number of legal and regulatory issues are associated with Internet business, global transmissions and transborder data flows (e.g., privacy, tax laws and tariffs, data import/export restrictions, warrants or subpoenas, restrictions on cryptography, warranties, patents, copyrights, trade secrets and national security). These vary depending upon the enterprise's location and may impose constraints and boundaries on security strategies. Research into these areas must be undertaken in conjunction with legal and regulatory departments and any areas of the business that may be affected.

texts.orig: 1.3.1 Requirements for Content and Retention of Business Records
texts.text: 1.3.1 Requirements for Content and Retention of Business Records

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Business records constitute a large subset of the information to be protected by the security strategy that will be developed, so it is important for the information security manager to understand the underlying requirements regarding those records. As one who provides input for creating the strategy, the information security manager must understand the business requirements regarding all types of enterprise records. Often, representatives from the enterprise legal department can help determine what types of records must be protected to ensure their confidentiality, integrity and availability. The legal affairs representatives can also provide information regarding legal and regulatory requirements for enterprise documents (including electronic messages and files).

As one who provides input for creating the strategy, the information security manager must understand the business requirements regarding all types of enterprise records. Often, representatives from the enterprise legal department can help determine what types of records must be protected to ensure their confidentiality, integrity and availability. The legal affairs representatives can also provide information regarding legal and regulatory requirements for enterprise documents (including electronic messages and files).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Business requirements may exceed the legal and regulatory requirements imposed by applicable legislating bodies due to the nature of the enterprise's business. Some enterprises have business needs requiring access to data that are 10 to 20 years old, or more. This type of data can include, for example, customer records, patient records and engineering information. As a rule, the retention strategy and subsequent policy must, at a minimum, meet the legal requirements in the applicable jurisdiction and industry.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Regulations such as Sarbanes-Oxley4 have imposed various mandatory retention requirements for various types and categories of information, regardless of the storage medium. The enterprise's retention strategy will require the information security manager to stay current with these requirements and ensure compliance. There may also be requirements stemming from any lawful preservation order that would require an enterprise or individual to retain specific data at the behest of law enforcement or other authorities. It is also generally the case that archived information must be indexed sufficiently to be located and retrieved.
texts.text: Regulations such as Sarbanes-Oxley4 have imposed various mandatory retention requirements for various types and categories of information, regardless of the storage medium. The enterprise's retention strategy will require the information security manager to stay current with these requirements and ensure compliance. There may also be requirements stemming from any lawful preservation order that would require an enterprise or individual to retain specific data at the behest of law enforcement or other authorities. It is also generally the case that archived information must be indexed sufficiently to be located and retrieved.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Increasingly, civil and criminal actions rely on evidence obtained from email and other electronic communications in response to a production request or subpoena. If information has been archived without being classified and cataloged, retrieving the required material can be an arduous and expensive task, as a number of high-profile cases have shown. The increasing prevalence of this type of discovery contributes to the need for careful consideration of a retention policy that limits the length of time—within the bounds of legal requirements—that certain information, such as email, is retained. Generally, the best option is to have a policy that requires destruction of any data not required to be retained by law or for specific business reasons.

If these attributes are not in place, strategy activities might include working with enterprise stakeholders to incorporate them. Key considerations for an effective organizational structure:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An examination of the organizational hierarchy and structure within the enterprise will enable the information security manager to understand the various stakeholders involved in the coordination, creation and management of the information security strategy. Notably, that hierarchy may not always be intuitive. The tendency to segment security into separate but related functions has created the need to integrate a variety of assurance processes found in a typical enterprise. These activities are often fragmented and segmented in silos with different reporting structures. The terminology associated with these activities generally reflects different understandings of processes and outcomes, at times with little in common. These assurance silos can include risk management, change management, internal and external audit, privacy offices, insurance offices, HR, legal and others. Evaluating business processes from start to finish (along with their controls), regardless of which particular assurance process is involved, can mitigate the tendency for security gaps to exist in various assurance functions.

texts.orig: Convergence is another structural consideration. Security-related activities are sometimes divided into separate divisions, such as physical security, IT security, risk management, privacy, compliance and information security. This approach has not been conducive to achieving optimal results, leading professionals and managers to reconsider this separation. The chief information security officer (CISO) may be elevated to chief security officer (CSO), with responsibility for a broad range of risk types, which can help to better integrate security elements. Integration of both the roles and infrastructure for physical security and information security is becoming commonplace. Because it is not possible to effectively deliver information security without a number of physical considerations, the evolution is natural. It is reasonable to expect that integration of many security activities will center around information security in the coming decade. As a result, integration of physical security and other assurance functions will be an increasingly relevant consideration for management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As new technologies emerge and threats become increasingly complex and unpredictable, senior security executives recognize the need to merge security functions throughout the entire enterprise. An incident at the Sumitomo Mitsui Bank in London, England, in which hackers attempted to steal £229 million from the bank, underlies this principle.5 Even though the bank had strong IT security measures in place, a physical security lapse occurred. Adversaries posing as janitors installed devices on computer keyboards (i.e., keyloggers) that allowed them to obtain valuable login information. This incident highlights and reinforces the need to converge all components of an enterprise's security through an integrated and deliberate approach. To be effective, a converged approach should reach across people, processes and technology, and enable enterprises to prevent, detect, respond to and recover from any type of security incident.

texts.text: 1.4.1 Roles and Responsibilities

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Clear definitions, both of organizational roles and of the responsibilities of those who hold them, are key to effective information security governance. Because everyone in the enterprise has some information security responsibilities, it is essential to clearly define them and communicate those responsibilities throughout the enterprise on a recurring basis.
texts.text: Clear definitions, both of organizational roles and of the responsibilities of those who hold them, are key to effective information security governance. Because everyone in the enterprise has some information security responsibilities, it is essential to clearly define them and communicate those responsibilities throughout the enterprise on a recurring basis.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A role is a designation assigned to an individual by virtue of a job function or other label. A responsibility is a description of some procedure or function related to the role that someone is accountable to perform. Roles are important to information security because they enable responsibilities and access rights to be assigned based on the function an individual performs rather than to specific individuals. There are typically many job functions in the enterprise that support security functions, and the ability to assign access authorizations based on roles simplifies administration.

texts.text: Board of Directors

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Board members need to be aware of the enterprise's information assets, risk to those assets and their criticality to ongoing business operations. The board should periodically be provided with the high-level results of comprehensive risk assessments and business impact analyses (BIAs). This information should inform board members in validating/ratifying the key assets they want protected and ensuring that protection levels and priorities are appropriate to a standard of due care.

This information should inform board members in validating/ratifying the key assets they want protected and ensuring that protection levels and priorities are appropriate to a standard of due care.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Security expectations should be met at all levels of the enterprise. Penalties for noncompliance must be defined, communicated and enforced from the board level down.
texts.text: Security expectations should be met at all levels of the enterprise. Penalties for noncompliance must be defined, communicated and enforced from the board level down.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Beyond these requirements, the board has an ongoing obligation to provide a level of oversight with respect to information security activities. Given the legal and ethical responsibility of directors to exercise due care in protecting the enterprise's key assets, which include its confidential and other critical information, an ongoing level of information security involvement and oversight is required.
texts.text: Beyond these requirements, the board has an ongoing obligation to provide a level of oversight with respect to information security activities. Given the legal and ethical responsibility of directors to exercise due care in protecting the enterprise's key assets, which include its confidential and other critical information, an ongoing level of information security involvement and oversight is required.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There are specific reasons that mandate the board of directors involvement with and oversight of information security activities. A common concern is liability. Most enterprises, to protect themselves from shareholder lawsuits, provide specific insurance to create a level of protection for the board in exercising its governance responsibilities. However, a typical requirement of this insurance is that directors make a good faith effort to exercise due care in the discharge of their duties. Neglecting to address information security risk may constitute a failure to exercise due care and may void the protection provided by insurance.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The US Sarbanes-Oxley Act mandates that every company listed on a US stock exchange maintain an audit committee with a required level of experience and demonstrable competence. This committee is often comprised of members of the company's board of directors. One of the committee's key responsibilities is the ongoing monitoring of the enterprise's internal controls that directly affect the reliability of financial statements. Most financial controls are technical and procedural, with the technical portion generally under the scope of the information security manager. It is important for the security manager to maintain an open channel of communication with this committee.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Institutional investors and others have come to understand that the long-term prospects for an enterprise are heavily impacted by the overall state of governance. Corporate rating enterprises provide a governance rating or metric based on a number of factors. Failure to provide an adequate level of governance and support for activities that protect the major assets of the enterprise is likely to be reflected in those scores. The weight and relevance of the scores will be driven by the consequences for enterprises that suffer the loss of significant critical and sensitive information. The bottom line is that a board of directors should provide direction, oversight and requirements for appropriate metrics. A 2019 meeting of the National Association of Corporate Directors Risk Oversight Advisory Council affirmed that cyber-risk reporting to the board should evolve to keep pace with the changing needs of the enterprise and of the board itself.⁶

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Security affects all aspects of an enterprise to some extent and must be pervasive throughout the enterprise to be effective. To ensure that all stakeholders impacted by security considerations are involved, many enterprises form a steering committee comprised of senior representatives of affected groups. The steering committee helps to achieve consensus on priorities and trade-offs. It serves as an effective communications channel and ensures the security program is aligned with business objectives. It can also be instrumental in achieving modification of behavior toward a culture more conducive to good security.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All enterprises have a CISO, regardless of whether anyone officially holds that title. It may be the chief information officer (CIO), chief security officer (CSO), chief financial officer (CFO) or chief executive officer (CEO). Legal responsibility will extend up the command structure by default and ultimately reside with senior management and the board of directors. It usually results in a lack of effective alignment of security activities with organizational objectives.

texts.text: Risk Management Roles and Responsibilities

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Managing risk effectively at an acceptable cost is the basis for the objectives and drivers of information security governance and programs to implement, develop and manage it. While risk management is ultimately a responsibility of senior management and the board of directors, everyone in an enterprise has a role to play. It is important that all risk management activities be integrated and operate under a consistent set of rules and clear objectives. This will help prevent gaps in protection, provide a more consistent level of protection, reduce needless redundant efforts and help keep different parts of the enterprise from operating at cross purposes.

texts.text: Part B: Information Security Strategy

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security governance is the responsibility of the board of directors and senior management. It must be an integral and transparent part of enterprise governance and complement or encompass the IT governance framework. While senior management has the responsibility to consider and respond to increasingly complex and potentially destructive information security issues, boards of directors will be required to make information security an intrinsic part of governance, integrated with the processes they have in place to govern other critical organizational resources. These include monitoring and reporting processes to ensure that governance is effective and that compliance enforcement is sufficient to reduce risk to acceptable levels.

texts.orig: To demonstrate capability maturity model integration (CMMI®), a strategy should include methods for ensuring an integrated and repeatable approach to governance and management. To optimize value, risk and resources, everyone in the enterprise needs to work together. Many of the processes described in this guide foster collaboration among various business areas; this collaboration can be improved and maintained using many of the practices described in the integrated CMMI product suite. ISACA's CMMI models have expanded beyond software engineering to help enterprises around the world, in any industry, understand their current level of capability and performance and offer a guide to optimize business results. Thus, CMMI provides a helpful input for creating a strategy that is repeatable, predictable and consistent.

Strategy is the plan to achieve an objective. The strategic direction of the business is defined by the objectives set forth in the strategy. To be of value to the enterprise, information security must support the business strategy and the activities that take place to achieve the objectives.

texts.orig: When the basic information security/risk management strategy is formulated, a logical architecture showing the various functions and data flows can be developed. A road map can then be laid out with the specific steps needed to attain the goals defined in the strategy. The specifics include the control objectives necessary to achieve acceptable risk levels. Some of these objectives will best be achieved with technologies defined in the physical architecture. The physical architecture consists of specific devices, such as servers, databases, firewalls, switches and routers, along with their interconnections. Controls must be developed that are consistent with the standards, and control choices will affect the specifics of both the physical and the operational architectures. Both the strategy and information security procedures are input into the operational architecture.

texts.orig: Most enterprises fail to define the objectives of information security with any specificity. This may be because it seems obvious that the goal of information security is to protect the enterprise's information assets. However, that answer assumes knowledge of two things. One is that information assets are known with any degree of precision, which for most enterprises is not the case. The other is that there is an assumed understanding of what it means "to protect." Everyone understands the notion in general. It is considerably more difficult to state which assets need how much protection against what.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In part, this is because the enterprise typically has insufficient knowledge of what information exists within it. There is generally no process to purge useless, outdated or potentially dangerous information, data or unused applications. It is extremely rare to find a comprehensive catalog or index of information/processes to define what is important, what is not important or who owns what. As a result, everything typically gets saved, under the assumption that storage is cheaper than data classification, ownership assignment and the identification of users. For large enterprises, this can amount to terabytes of useless data and literally thousands of outdated and unused applications accumulated over decades.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Assuming relevant information is located and identified, it must be classified by criticality and sensitivity or business value. Classification provides the basis for applying protective measures in proportion to the business value, resulting in more cost-effective controls. Because a great deal of a typical enterprise's data and information are neither critical nor sensitive, it is wasteful to expend substantial resources to protect them. For many enterprises, locating and classifying information assets may be a significant undertaking, and there is often a reluctance to allocate the resources necessary. However, this is a crucial step in developing a practical and useful information security strategy and a cost-effective security program.

texts.orig: Just as values are assigned to an enterprise's physical resources, values must be assigned to information to prioritize budget-constrained protection efforts and determine required levels of protection. Valuation of information is difficult to do with any precision. For some information, it can be the cost of creating or replacing it. In other cases, information in the form of knowledge or trade secrets is difficult or impossible to replace and may be priceless. It is obviously prudent to provide strong protection to priceless information.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One approach commonly used is to create a few rough levels of value—for example, from zero to five, with zero being of no value and five being critical. The zerovalue would be assigned to information, including applications, if no owner could be determined and no use occurred for a period of time. Information of zero value could then be archived for a specified period, notices could be sent to business owners and, if there were no objections, it could be destroyed. Information deemed a five (critical) would be given the highest priority for protection efforts proportional to the other valuations.

The contribution these resources make to revenue provides a measure of the level of their criticality, which can be used as a guide for protection efforts.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For most enterprises, asset classification is a daunting task, but one that must be undertaken for existing information if security governance is to be effective, efficient and relevant. Done correctly, classification mitigates the cost of overprotecting unimportant information and the risk of underprotecting high-value information. This task grows exponentially more onerous over time if it is not addressed. Policies, standards and processes must be developed concurrently to mandate classification moving forward and prevent related problems from getting worse. Overclassification is a serious problem for classification implementation. It can be particularly troublesome in enterprises with a blame culture, where mistakes are not well tolerated. In such environments, data owners may err on the side of caution by marking data more sensitive or critical than warranted, negating the potential benefits of classification. There is a practical solution for enterprises where IT operates on a chargeback system and IT services are a cost to the business units. In such cases, additional charges for higher classifications will tend to counteract the tendency to overclassify.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If an information security strategy is the basis for a plan of action to achieve security objectives, it is necessary to define those objectives. Defining long-term objectives in terms of a desired state of security is necessary for a number of reasons. Without a well-articulated vision of desired outcomes for a security program, it will not be possible to develop a meaningful strategy.

Defining long-term objectives in terms of a desired state of security is necessary for a number of reasons. Without a well-articulated vision of desired outcomes for a security program, it will not be possible to develop a meaningful strategy.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Without a strategy, it is not possible to develop a meaningful plan of action and the enterprise will continue to implement ad hoc tactical point solutions with nothing to provide overall integration. The resulting nonintegrated systems will be increasingly difficult to manage and will become ever more costly and difficult or impossible to secure.

texts.orig: A review of the enterprise's strategic business plans is likely to uncover opportunities for information security activities that can enable or be directly supportive of a particular avenue of business by reducing risk, losses and potential operational disruptions. Other sources of information to guide security efforts include change management activities, audit reports and steering committee discussions. As an example, the implementation of a public key infrastructure (PKI) can enable high-value transactions between trusted trading partners or customers. Deploying virtual private networks (VPNs) may provide the sales force with secure remote connectivity, enabling strong protection for sensitive information. In other words, information security can enable business activities that would otherwise be too risky to undertake or, as frequently happens, are undertaken with the hope that nothing will go wrong.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In determining strategic objectives, it is essential to ensure there are direct linkages to specific business activities and goals. These linkages can start from the perspective of a particular line of business, taking its specific objectives into account. A review and analysis of all the elements of a particular product line can illustrate how this approach might work.
texts.text: In determining strategic objectives, it is essential to ensure there are direct linkages to specific business activities and goals. These linkages can start from the perspective of a particular line of business, taking its specific objectives into account. A review and analysis of all the elements of a particular product line can illustrate how this approach might work.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Consider an enterprise that manufactures breakfast cereal. The raw materials come into the plant on a justin-time basis via railcar. The grains are dumped into hoppers that feed the various processing machinery. The finished cereals are packaged and moved to a warehouse in a continuous, highly automated process in a matter of hours.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This relatively straightforward process relies on numerous information flows that are subject to a failure of confidentiality, integrity or availability. Any breakdown or significant disruption in the systems that support the supply chain side (e.g., ordering, tracking or payments) is likely to cause a disruption in manufacturing. All the automated processing activities in the plant are tied to data processing and information flows. Any interruption or corruption of data would cause a failure of the process, ranging from stopping manufacturing to delivering defective product. An effective information security program must be based on an understanding and consideration of all the information streams that are critical to ensuring continuous operations. Obviously, anything that can negatively affect the integrity or availability of the information needed in this continuous and interdependent process will be a problem. The linkage to the business, in this case, is the ability of an effective security program to prevent disruptions to the information systems essential to production.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: COBIT provides a comprehensive framework for the governance and management of enterprise IT and extensively addresses IT security, governance, risk and information security in general. Because many aspects of information security involve IT and related activities, it can serve as a framework for determining the desired state for effective information security. COBIT includes several focus areas that describe a particular governance topic, domain or issue that can be addressed by a collection of governance and management objectives and their components. Examples of potential focus areas include small and medium enterprises, information security, risk, digital transformation, cloud computing, privacy and DevOps. Focus areas may contain a combination of generic governance components and variants and provide input considerations for information security governance.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The BMIS model uses systems thinking to clarify complex relationships within the enterprise to more effectively manage security. The elements and dynamic interconnections that form the basis of the model establish the boundaries of an information security program and model how the program functions and reacts to internal and external change. BMIS provides the context for frameworks such as COBIT.

texts.orig: A system needs to be viewed holistically—not merely as a sum of its parts—to be accurately understood. This is the essence of systems theory. A holistic approach examines the system as a complete functioning unit. Another tenet of systems theory is that one part of the system enables understanding of other parts of the system. "Systems thinking" is a widely recognized term that refers to the examination of how systems interact, how complex systems work and why "the whole is more than the sum of its parts."

"Systems thinking" is a widely recognized term that refers to the examination of how systems interact, how complex systems work and why "the whole is more than the sum of its parts."

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Systems theory encompasses a complex network of events, relationships, reactions, consequences, technologies, processes and people interacting in often unseen and unexpected ways. Studying the behaviors and results of the interactions can assist managers to better understand the organizational system and the way it functions. While management of any discipline within the enterprise can be enhanced by approaching it from a systems thinking perspective, its implementation will certainly help with managing risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The success the systems approach has achieved in other fields bodes well for the benefits it can bring to security. The often dramatic failures of enterprises to adequately address security issues in recent years are due, to a significant extent, to their inability to define security and present it in a way that is comprehensible and relevant to all stakeholders. Using a systems approach to information security management will help information security managers address complex and dynamic environments and will generate a beneficial effect on collaboration within the enterprise, adaptation to operational change, navigation of strategic uncertainty and tolerance of the impact of external factors.

The dynamic interconnections act as tensions, exerting a push/pull force in reaction to changes in the enterprise, allowing the model to adapt as needed.

texts.text: 1.5.6 Information Security Strategy Development

texts.label: text
texts.orig: With the information described in the previous section, a meaningful security strategy can be developed—a strategy to move from the current state to the desired state. Knowing where one is and where one is going provides the essential starting point for strategy development; it provides the framework for creating a road map. The road map essentially delineates the specific steps that must be taken to implement the strategy.
texts.text: With the information described in the previous section, a meaningful security strategy can be developed—a strategy to move from the current state to the desired state. Knowing where one is and where one is going provides the essential starting point for strategy development; it provides the framework for creating a road map. The road map essentially delineates the specific steps that must be taken to implement the strategy.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security objectives, coupled with available processes, methods, tools and techniques, create the means to construct a security strategy. A good security strategy should address and mitigate risk while providing an acceptable level of compliance with the legal, contractual and statutory requirements of the enterprise. It should provide demonstrable support for its business objectives and maximize value to stakeholders. The security strategy also needs to address how the enterprise will embed good security practices into every business process and area.
texts.text: Information security objectives, coupled with available processes, methods, tools and techniques, create the means to construct a security strategy. A good security strategy should address and mitigate risk while providing an acceptable level of compliance with the legal, contractual and statutory requirements of the enterprise. It should provide demonstrable support for its business objectives and maximize value to stakeholders. The security strategy also needs to address how the enterprise will embed good security practices into every business process and area.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Often, those charged with developing a security strategy think in terms of controls as the means to implement security. Controls, while important, are not the only element available to the strategist. In some cases, reengineering a process can reduce or eliminate a risk without the need for controls. Potential impacts may be mitigated by architectural modifications rather than controls. Another consideration is that mitigating risk can sometimes reduce business opportunities to the extent that it becomes counterproductive. It is essential to consider how risk mitigation activities impact productivity so that a careful balance can be struck between security and operational efficiency/effectiveness. This can generally be accomplished by performing a cost-benefit analysis of proposed control activities.

texts.orig: 1.6 Information Governance Frameworks and Standards
texts.text: 1.6 Information Governance Frameworks and Standards

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To achieve effective information security governance, management must establish and ensure maintenance of a framework to guide the development and management of a comprehensive information security program that supports the business objectives.
texts.text: To achieve effective information security governance, management must establish and ensure maintenance of a framework to guide the development and management of a comprehensive information security program that supports the business objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The governance framework will generally consist of the following:
texts.text: The governance framework will generally consist of the following:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: A comprehensive security strategy intrinsically linked with business objectives
texts.text: A comprehensive security strategy intrinsically linked with business objectives

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Governing security policies that clearly express management intent and address each aspect of strategy, controls and regulation
texts.text: Governing security policies that clearly express management intent and address each aspect of strategy, controls and regulation

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: A complete set of standards for each policy to ensure that people, procedures, practices and technologies comply with policy requirements and set appropriate security baselines for the enterprise
texts.text: A complete set of standards for each policy to ensure that people, procedures, practices and technologies comply with policy requirements and set appropriate security baselines for the enterprise

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: An effective security organizational structure with sufficient authority and adequate resources, void of conflicts of interest
texts.text: An effective security organizational structure with sufficient authority and adequate resources, void of conflicts of interest

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Detailed workflows and structures that assist in defining responsibilities and accountability for information security governance
texts.text: Detailed workflows and structures that assist in defining responsibilities and accountability for information security governance

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Institutionalized metrics and monitoring processes to ensure compliance, provide feedback on control effectiveness and provide the basis for making appropriate management decisions
texts.text: Institutionalized metrics and monitoring processes to ensure compliance, provide feedback on control effectiveness and provide the basis for making appropriate management decisions

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This framework provides the basis for developing a costeffective information security program that supports the enterprise's business goals. Implementing and managing a security program is covered in Chapter 3. The objective of the program is a set of activities that provide assurance that information assets are given a level of protection commensurate with their business value or with the risk their compromise poses to the enterprise. The relationships among IT, information security, controls, architecture and the other components of a governance framework are represented in figure 1.11. While linkage between IT and information security may occur at various higher levels, strategy is the point where information security must integrate IT to achieve its objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Enterprise information security architecture (EISA) is a subset of enterprise architecture. An architecture framework can be described as a foundational structure, or set of structures, that can be used for developing a broad range of different architectures, including business process architecture—sometimes referred to as the contextual architecture——and the more traditional conceptual, logical, physical, functional and operational architectures.
texts.text: Enterprise information security architecture (EISA) is a subset of enterprise architecture. An architecture framework can be described as a foundational structure, or set of structures, that can be used for developing a broad range of different architectures, including business process architecture—sometimes referred to as the contextual architecture——and the more traditional conceptual, logical, physical, functional and operational architectures.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Many methodologies have evolved, including process models, frameworks and ad hoc approaches favored by some consultancies. This evolution occurred as it became evident that an architectural perspective limited to IT was inadequate to address business design and development of security requirements.
texts.text: Many methodologies have evolved, including process models, frameworks and ad hoc approaches favored by some consultancies. This evolution occurred as it became evident that an architectural perspective limited to IT was inadequate to address business design and development of security requirements.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A number of architectural approaches now provide linkages to the business side of information protection and methods for its design. Architectural approaches that are inclusive of business processes that may be appropriate for defining the desired state of security include (but are not limited to) framework models such as COBIT, the Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF), the Zachman Enterprise Architecture Framework, and the Extended Enterprise Architecture Framework (E2AF). These models can define most or all of the desired state of security, provided they are properly used to reflect and implement the organizational security strategy.

texts.orig: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
texts.text: NIST Cybersecurity Framework

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Formally titled the NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework provides high-level guidance for aligning a cybersecurity program with enterprise objectives. In response to an increasing prevalence of cybersecurity attacks, NIST convened a series of workshops to develop a process by which an enterprise could identify opportunities for improvement in the information security program. The framework highlights the need for effective risk management integration and it broadly supports improvement in supply chain risk management.
texts.text: Formally titled the NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework provides high-level guidance for aligning a cybersecurity program with enterprise objectives. In response to an increasing prevalence of cybersecurity attacks, NIST convened a series of workshops to develop a process by which an enterprise could identify opportunities for improvement in the information security program. The framework highlights the need for effective risk management integration and it broadly supports improvement in supply chain risk management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework does not provide controls to be applied. Instead, it guides practitioners through the process of determining gaps between the current state of practice and a desired target state that might better fulfill their enterprise mission, including risk management needs. Analysis of the gaps between states enables the use of controls-based frameworks (including those listed herein) to improve information security risk management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It may be useful to employ a combination of methods to describe the desired state to assist in communications with others and as a way to cross-check the objectives to make certain all relevant elements are considered. For example, some combination of COBIT control objectives, CMMI, balanced scorecard and an appropriate architectural model would make a powerful combination. While it may seem like overkill, each approach presents a different viewpoint, and using them in combination is likely to ensure that no significant aspect is overlooked. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Although it was sufficient in the past for information security to report to the CIO, that structure has become inadequate for effectively addressing increased risk, growing losses and the sophistication of attackers. Further, it often results in a conflict of interest. As a result, information security increasingly has C-level management responsibilities and reports to the COO, CEO or the board of directors. There are several reasons for this. One is that the broad requirements of information security are outside the scope and focus of the typical CIO. Another reason is that the inherent conflict of interest resulting from information security is primarily a regulatory activity, while the CIO is often focused on cost and performance of IT. Information security, due to efforts to ensure security, is often perceived as a constraint on IT operations. CIOs and IT departments are usually under pressure to increase performance and cut costs, and a reduced security budget is usually a result of those pressures. Finally, for information security to be effective, it must be aligned with the business rather than with technology.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Finding employees with the necessary combination of security skills to be effective in an ever-changing, diverse environment and complex regulatory climate can be difficult and expensive. One way some enterprises attempt to ensure that all needed skills are available is to hire overqualified people. The concern with this approach is that these individuals are costly to acquire and maintain and, failing to be challenged, are often dissatisfied with the work. This can lead to excessive employee turnover, unproductive attitudes or substandard performance.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Security violations are an ongoing concern for information security managers, and it is important to develop procedures for handling them as a part of developing the strategy. Senior management buy-in and backing for these procedures are critical, especially in the area of enforcement. Security managers often find that the greatest compliance problems arise with management. If there is a lack of commitment and compliance in management ranks, it may be difficult, if not impossible, to enforce compliance across an enterprise.

texts.label: text

texts.label: text

In a typical enterprise, there are some policies and procedures that are more critical than others and, from a security perspective, may require 100 percent compliance (e.g., the operation of a nuclear power plant). Because it may not be practical, possible or cost-effective to monitor all compliance equally, prioritization of compliance requirements should focus on areas of greatest risk and impact.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Business dependency analysis is similar to resource dependency analysis but is less granular and includes elements that would be considered in a business continuity plan, such as staples and paper clips. Resource dependency is similar to disaster recovery planning in that it considers the systems, hardware and software required to perform specific organizational functions. Resource dependency can provide another perspective on the criticality of information resources. It can, to some extent, be used instead of an impact analysis to ensure that the strategy considers resources critical to business operations. The analysis is based on determining the resources (such as systems, software, connectivity) and dependencies (such as input processes and data repositories) required by operations critical to the enterprise.
texts.text: Business dependency analysis is similar to resource dependency analysis but is less granular and includes elements that would be considered in a business continuity plan, such as staples and paper clips. Resource dependency is similar to disaster recovery planning in that it considers the systems, hardware and software required to perform specific organizational functions. Resource dependency can provide another perspective on the criticality of information resources. texts.orig: Outsourced Services
texts.text: Outsourced Services

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Outsourcing is common, both onshore and offshore, as companies focus on core competencies and ways to cut costs. From an information security point of view, these arrangements can present risk that may be difficult to quantify and potentially difficult to mitigate. Typically, both the resources and skills of the outsourced functions are lost to the enterprise, which in itself presents risk. Providers may operate on different standards and can be difficult to control. The security strategy should ensure that outsourced security services are not a critical single point of failure and that there is a viable backup plan in the event of service provider failure.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While threat assessment is performed as part of overall risk assessment, it is an important element for strategic consideration by itself. One reason is that risk treatment options should consider the most cost-effective approach for addressing any particular risk. For example, mitigation measures can address threats directly, they can reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities, or they can address and compensate for impacts. The most costeffective choice is facilitated by separately analyzing threat, vulnerability, exposure and impact.

texts.orig: Vulnerability Assessment
texts.text: Vulnerability Assessment

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In most enterprises, technical vulnerability assessments using automated scans are common but by themselves are of limited value for security strategy development. Comprehensive vulnerability assessments that include physical elements——such as procedures, practices, technologies, facilities, service level agreements, and legal and contractual requirements—are essential. Processes and facilities are often the most vulnerable components; yet, because of the greater difficulty in assessing them, they are the least frequently assessed. The process of developing a strategy offers opportunities to address many vulnerabilities with a prudent, proactive approach. Even if no known or apparent threats exist for weaknesses discovered during these assessments, costeffective opportunities to address systemic weaknesses during strategy development should be considered. See Section 2.7.11 Vulnerabilities.

texts.orig: Insurance
texts.text: Insurance

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Strategy resources include the option of addressing some risk with insurance. Generally, the types of risk suitable for insuring are rare, high-impact events such as floods, hurricanes, fire, embezzlement or liability lawsuits. The most common types of insurance that can be considered include first-party, third-party and fidelity bonds. Firstparty insurance covers the enterprise in the event of damage from most sources, including business interruption, direct loss and recovery costs. Third-party insurance deals with potential liability to third parties. It generally includes defense against lawsuits and covers damages up to predetermined limits. Fidelity insurance or bonding involves protection against employee or agent theft or embezzlement.

texts.text: Other Organizational Support and Assurance Providers

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When developing a security strategy, a number of support and assurance service providers within an enterprise should be considered as part of information security resources. These can include a variety of departments, such as legal, compliance, audit, procurement, insurance, disaster recovery, physical security, training, project office and HR. Other departments or groups, such as change management or quality assurance, also have elements of assurance as a part of their operation.

texts.label: text

Strategic considerations include approaches to ensure that these functions operate seamlessly to prevent gaps that may lead to security compromises. The security strategy should aim to reduce or eliminate duplication of efforts and help prevent various groups working at cross-purposes (i.e., prevent the assurance activities of one group from undermining by the activities of another).
