texts.label: text
texts.orig: Considerations for information security metrics include ensuring that what is being measured is, in fact, relevant. Security is difficult to measure in any objective sense, and relatively meaningless metrics are often used simply because they are readily available. Metrics serve only one purpose: to provide the information necessary for making decisions. It is, therefore, critical to understand what decisions must be made and who makes them and then find ways of supplying that information in an accurate and timely fashion. Different metrics are more or less useful for different parts of the enterprise and should be determined in collaboration with business process owners and management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The CISO of a large manufacturing company with three years' experience has begun to realize that the information security function is having less influence and information risk recommendations are increasingly being ignored by the enterprise's business units. Despite continuing efforts to communicate with managers from the various corporate departments and business units and a positively regarded security training and awareness program, she has been having little success in getting management buy-in for implementing needed controls.
texts.text: The CISO of a large manufacturing company with three years' experience has begun to realize that the information security function is having less influence and information risk recommendations are increasingly being ignored by the enterprise's business units. Despite continuing efforts to communicate with managers from the various corporate departments and business units and a positively regarded security training and awareness program, she has been having little success in getting management buy-in for implementing needed controls.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The decreasing interest in information security became apparent when she was not invited to a series of meetings concerning significant changes in company operations. During subsequent budget meetings, several executives (including the CEO) said they were unsure of the value that information security contributed to the company and suggested the budget might be better allocated elsewhere. In addition, the CISO noticed that she had not been invited to a board meeting to present updates regarding the information security program in more than a year.

texts.orig: The company is publicly held and has been in operation for nearly 90 years. It has been profitable for all but a few years of its existence, although profits were down during the recent worldwide recession. The company has approximately 9,000 employees and a few hundred long-term contractors. It makes a wide variety of small hand and power tools and is known internationally for the wide variety of highquality products it makes.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 1. A. It is not possible to eliminate all vulnerabilities, and vulnerabilities that have no impact or exposure do not require the expenditure of resources to remediate or achieve elimination.
texts.text: A. It is not possible to eliminate all vulnerabilities, and vulnerabilities that have no impact or exposure do not require the expenditure of resources to remediate or achieve elimination.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. Reduction of risk to the lowest level generally is more costly and unnecessarily restrictive. The goal is to achieve control objectives that will result in acceptable levels of risk.
texts.text: Reduction of risk to the lowest level generally is more costly and unnecessarily restrictive. The goal is to achieve control objectives that will result in acceptable levels of risk.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. The objective of risk management is managing risk to a level acceptable to the enterprise.
texts.text: The objective of risk management is managing risk to a level acceptable to the enterprise.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. Countermeasures are a targeted control and a part of the risk treatment process to achieve the overall objective of risk management.
texts.text: Countermeasures are a targeted control and a part of the risk treatment process to achieve the overall objective of risk management.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 2. A. A regulatory requirement, regardless of whether it is mandated by the enterprise, should be treated as any other risk.
texts.text: A. A regulatory requirement, regardless of whether it is mandated by the enterprise, should be treated as any other risk.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. A regulatory requirement is a priority to the extent the level of risk compares to other risk. Priorities for risk management are usually based on probability and impact—the more likely the compromise and the more severe the consequences, the higher the priority.
texts.text: A regulatory requirement is a priority to the extent the level of risk compares to other risk. Priorities for risk management are usually based on probability and impact—the more likely the compromise and the more severe the consequences, the higher the priority.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. Regulatory compliance is not just an operational issue, but a management issue.
texts.text: Regulatory compliance is not just an operational issue, but a management issue.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. There are numerous regulations that may affect an enterprise. Priority wil be a management decision based on those regulations with the greatest level of enforcement (risk) and the most severe sanctions (consequences or impact) in addition to the cost of compliance (mitigation), just as with any other risk. In some cases, management may decide that the cost of potential sanctions will be less than the cost of compliance. While it is generally preferable to be as compliant as reasonably possible, the extent of regulatory compliance is a management decision, not a security decision. All risk must be prioritized, and compliance may not pose the greatest risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Risk management is a process aimed at achieving an optimal balance between realizing opportunities for gain, minimizing vulnerabilities and reducing the potential for loss. This is usually accomplished by ensuring that the impact of threats exploiting vulnerabilities is within acceptable limits at an acceptable cost. Risk management is different from managing risk, which is often used synonymously with risk mitigation or risk response/risk treatment.
texts.text: Risk management is a process aimed at achieving an optimal balance between realizing opportunities for gain, minimizing vulnerabilities and reducing the potential for loss. This is usually accomplished by ensuring that the impact of threats exploiting vulnerabilities is within acceptable limits at an acceptable cost. Risk management is different from managing risk, which is often used synonymously with risk mitigation or risk response/risk treatment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In practical business terms, risk management means that risk is managed so it does not materially impact the enterprise or catastrophically degrade a business process to a point beyond what has been deemed as acceptable. Risk is inherent in all activities; typically, a higher level of strategic risk will be taken to attempt to achieve higher returns. However, each enterprise needs to define its risk appetite and tolerance levels and ensure they are appropriate in order to achieve the organizational goals it wants to accomplish.
texts.text: In practical business terms, risk management means that risk is managed so it does not materially impact the enterprise or catastrophically degrade a business process to a point beyond what has been deemed as acceptable. Risk is inherent in all activities; typically, a higher level of strategic risk will be taken to attempt to achieve higher returns. However, each enterprise needs to define its risk appetite and tolerance levels and ensure they are appropriate in order to achieve the organizational goals it wants to accomplish.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The foundation for effective risk management is a comprehensive risk assessment, based on a solid understanding of the enterprise risk universe, which is ever-changing. It is not possible to devise a practical and relevant risk management program if there is no common understanding of the nature and extent of risk to information resources and the potential impact on the enterprise's activities. The structure of an enterprise's risk function can be centralized or decentralized. Mature enterprises generally manage risk through an enterprise risk management (ERM) group or department to ensure consistency. There may be instances in which enterprises have a separate IT risk department, whereas others have IT risk as a team under the ERM group. In some cases, the information security management, business resiliency and incident management programs may be integrated into an existing risk management program. In others, risk is managed by several departments and operational units, necessitating efforts to ensure continuity and integration of risk management activities.

texts.orig: Because risk management decisions typically have major financial implications and can require changes across the entire enterprise, it is imperative that senior management is supportive of the process and fully understands and agrees with the results of the program.

texts.orig: Risk management can mean different things to different people in the enterprise. For example, senior management may be looking only at the risk that would prevent the enterprise from executing its strategy and may have a difficult time justifying investing in controls to address threats that are perceived to have a low probability of occurrence. Business line managers might only look at threats to their operations and ability to meet their performance targets. An IT auditor's view may be that risk management means the prevention of loss, whereas an insurance manager could define it as cost-effective risk financing. It is critically important that the enterprise clearly provide its definition of risk management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The environment an enterprise operates in is constantly changing in multiple aspects, including business, geopolitical, regulatory, statutory and how technologies are being used. The potential threats and resulting risks to the enterprise are also evolving. For example, the COVID pandemic triggered the wide-scale movement of employees from workplaces to working remotely. The information security manager should be aware of and monitor these changes in terms of how they may impact the enterprise's information assets, business processes, ability to demonstrate compliance, privacy, security and risk overall.

texts.text: 2.1.1 Risk Identification

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Before an enterprise can look into potential and emerging risk, it is important to know how to identify risk. Risk identification is the process by which the type and nature of viable threats are determined and the enterprise's vulnerabilities that are subject to those threats are examined. The vulnerabilities that may be exploited by the identified threats constitute identified risk. The process of risk identification is essential to effective risk management because only identified risk can be assessed and treated appropriately.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Risk identification is often accomplished through a knowledgeable group developing a variety of risk scenarios or brainstorming sessions (i.e., structured what-if techniques, diagramming techniques). These exercises assume that all significant vulnerabilities of the enterprise are known and the type and nature of threats that could exploit them are identified. Vulnerabilities take many forms. They may be commonly understood technical weaknesses, or they may be obscured by business processes or unmonitored procedures. A lack of awareness by staff can also create vulnerabilities, such as exposure of information via conversations in public spaces (e.g., elevators or restaurants) that could be overheard or via leaks to social media. Outsourced services are a source of vulnerabilities that may be difficult to determine.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Threats to information resources and the likelihood that they will exploit an existing vulnerability must be assessed. In this context, threats are any circumstances or events with the potential to cause harm to an information resource by exploiting vulnerabilities in the system.
texts.text: Threats to information resources and the likelihood that they will exploit an existing vulnerability must be assessed. In this context, threats are any circumstances or events with the potential to cause harm to an information resource by exploiting vulnerabilities in the system.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Threats may be the result of accidental actions, intentional/deliberate actions or natural events. Threats may originate from either internal or external sources, and actual attacks may leverage a combination of both internal and external sources. They may be caused by natural events or political, economic or competitive factors. Threats always exist and are typically beyond the direct control of the enterprise. Not all conceivable threats need to be considered by every enterprise. For example, an enterprise that operates in a region with a seismic rating of zero might not be inclined to invest their efforts in documenting exposure to volcanoes or earthquakes. However, it is important to identify the various types of threats that do apply and may compromise systems or otherwise affect the enterprise.

texts.orig: Internal Threats
texts.text: Internal Threats

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Although many enterprises label their employees and other staff as their best asset, they may be unhappy if inadequately trained, treated poorly or not given enough time to do their jobs properly. Disillusionment and resentment can lead to a higher risk of errors, negligence and more conscious actions such as theft. Key personnel may be drawn to another company and leave serious gaps in the knowledge and skills needed to operate systems effectively.
texts.text: Although many enterprises label their employees and other staff as their best asset, they may be unhappy if inadequately trained, treated poorly or not given enough time to do their jobs properly. Disillusionment and resentment can lead to a higher risk of errors, negligence and more conscious actions such as theft. Key personnel may be drawn to another company and leave serious gaps in the knowledge and skills needed to operate systems effectively.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Employees are the cause of a significant number of business impacts, which can be intentional and unintentional. A disgruntled employee may intentionally compromise systems or release data that expose the enterprise to legal or reputational risk. Employees may be convinced, bribed or threatened to disclose trade secrets for ideological or economic reasons. Many employees have a level of access to systems and data that far exceeds their actual job requirements, which can be used and exploited in an attack. The solution to the employee problem, therefore, lies at least in part in the application of need-to-know and least privilege and segregation of duties (SoD), but this is an imperfect solution. Any system has trusted insiders, and one of them choosing to violate trust is difficult to either predict or prevent.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The typical profile of a malicious insider is a current or former employee, contractor or other business partner who has or once had authorized access to an enterprise's network, system or data and intentionally intercepted, exfiltrated, interrupted, modified or fabricated data on the enterprise's information systems. The first step in addressing personnel threats is to start with the hiring process and review the qualifications and attitude of prospective employees. Employment candidates may submit incorrect information on job applications and claim education, certification or experience they do not actually possess. A review of references and performance of background checks may be worthwhile to the extent permitted by law. At the time of hiring, the employee should be required to sign a nondisclosure agreement (NDA) and be advised of the ethics and policies of the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Throughout employment, employees should be reminded of organizational policies and their responsibilities through awareness sessions and regular management reviews. One of the best employee-based controls is to actively engage with employees to understand any frustrations, complaints or issues they may be facing and then seek to resolve those issues. During times of strike, layoffs, mergers, acquisitions, relocation and reorganization, an employee's threat profile is more likely to increase—and by extension, the associated risk. An employee who has been recently demoted or bypassed for a promotion may also pose a risk.

texts.orig: Advanced Persistent Threats
texts.text: Advanced Persistent Threats

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) refers to advanced, highly skilled attackers who are sufficiently motivated to exploit systems and networks. The increased skills available to the hacking community and the effectiveness of the tools they possess make the risk of compromise much more significant. APTs may be sponsored by governments, organized crime or competitors. The information security manager must be aware that APTs pose a significant risk to enterprises of virtually all types globally and ensure that appropriate steps are in place to detect and identify this threat.
texts.text: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) refers to advanced, highly skilled attackers who are sufficiently motivated to exploit systems and networks. The increased skills available to the hacking community and the effectiveness of the tools they possess make the risk of compromise much more significant. APTs may be sponsored by governments, organized crime or competitors. The information security manager must be aware that APTs pose a significant risk to enterprises of virtually all types globally and ensure that appropriate steps are in place to detect and identify this threat.

texts.orig: APT is defined by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) as follows'⁵:
texts.text: APT is defined by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) as follows'⁵:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An APT is an adversary that possesses sophisticated levels of expertise and significant resources which allow it to create opportunities to achieve its objectives using multiple attack vectors (e.g., cyber, physical and deception). These objectives typically include establishing and extending footholds within the IT infrastructure of the targeted organizations for purposes of exfiltrating information, undermining or impeding critical aspects of a mission, program or organization; or positioning itself to carry out these objectives in the future. The advanced persistent threat: (i) pursues its objectives repeatedly over an extended period of time; (ii) adapts to defenders'efforts to resist it; and (iii) is determined to maintain the level of interaction needed to execute its objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The framework for risk management establishes the basic parameters within which risk must be managed are defined, including the criteria for acceptable risk and control objectives. Consequently, the scope for the rest of the risk management process is also set. It includes the definition of basic assumptions for the enterprise's external and internal environment and the overall objectives of the risk management process and activities. Although the definition of scope and framework are fundamental for the establishment of risk management, they are independent of the particular structure of the management process, methods and tools to be used for the implementation.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Indications of emerging threats may include unusual activity on a system, repeated alarms, slow system or network performance, or new or excessive activity in logs. In many cases, compromised enterprises have evidence of emergent threats in their logs well in advance of the actual compromise, but the evidence is not noticed or acted on. Lack of effective monitoring, when combined with a threat, can lead to a breach.

texts.orig: Most technologies are built with an emphasis on function and purpose without due consideration for the security implications. As a result, new technology tends to be a source of new vulnerabilities and may even itself be a threat agent within an information system. The information security manager must be alert to the emergence of new technologies and prepare for their introduction into the enterprise, particularly if the technologies promise cost savings or competitive advantage.

The information security manager must be alert to the emergence of new technologies and prepare for their introduction into the enterprise, particularly if the technologies promise cost savings or competitive advantage.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Bring your own device (BYOD) is an example of a revolution in the way enterprises view technology assets. It is an opportunity with self-evident risk, yet it has tempted a wide variety of enterprises by promising to greatly reduce the cost of initial procurement of IT assets and the rate at which they need to be refreshed. A threat strategy that emphasizes rejection of new technology is unlikely to remain in place for long after it gains executive sponsorship.

New sets of risk-reducing processes, staff and technologies that had not been previously considered may be required to reduce residual risk to acceptable levels.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The explosive growth of various smart technologies, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled devices and edge computing enable a model in which devices are located and information is processed in the periphery of the network, physically closer to user locations. This decentralized model differs from the traditional data center paradigm, and information security managers need to take into account the associated risk and consider the required controls to address and reduce risk and ensure it aligns with the enterprise's defined risk appetite and tolerance.

texts.orig: 2.1.5 Risk, Likelihood and Impact
texts.text: 2.1.5 Risk, Likelihood and Impact

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The International Organization of Standardization (ISO) defines risk as "the effect of uncertainty on objectives."16 This means that outcomes could have either a positive or negative result. In this publication, risk will be considered from primarily a negative perspective, where negative risk is defined as "the probability of an event (uncertainty) and its consequences (impact to objectives)."
texts.text: The International Organization of Standardization (ISO) defines risk as "the effect of uncertainty on objectives."16 This means that outcomes could have either a positive or negative result. In this publication, risk will be considered from primarily a negative perspective, where negative risk is defined as "the probability of an event (uncertainty) and its consequences (impact to objectives)."

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The likelihood, or probability, is a measure of the frequency that an event may occur. When identifying risk, likelihood is used to calculate the level of risk based on the frequency of events, combined with the impact of those events that may occur in a given time period (e.g., a year). The likelihood or frequency combined with the magnitude (of impact) is used in determining annual loss expectancy (ALE). The greater the frequency, the greater the likelihood and, consequently, the greater the risk. See Section 2.3.8 Risk Analysis for more information.
texts.text: The likelihood, or probability, is a measure of the frequency that an event may occur. When identifying risk, likelihood is used to calculate the level of risk based on the frequency of events, combined with the impact of those events that may occur in a given time period (e.g., a year). The likelihood or frequency combined with the magnitude (of impact) is used in determining annual loss expectancy (ALE). The greater the frequency, the greater the likelihood and, consequently, the greater the risk. See Section 2.3.8 Risk Analysis for more information.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When discussing risk, it is important to acknowledge the subtle differences between likelihood and probability. Likelihood is an expected frequency of occurrence, meaning how many times an event may occur over a specified interval (weeks, months, years). Probability is described in a range from 0 to 1; in other words, an event may or may not occur. When identifying risk, the level of risk is calculated based on its likelihood and probability, in combination with the impact that may occur within a given time period (e.g., a year). The greater the likelihood (or frequency of occurrence) and the resulting outcome (or consequence/impact), the greater the risk.
texts.text: When discussing risk, it is important to acknowledge the subtle differences between likelihood and probability. Likelihood is an expected frequency of occurrence, meaning how many times an event may occur over a specified interval (weeks, months, years). Probability is described in a range from 0 to 1; in other words, an event may or may not occur. When identifying risk, the level of risk is calculated based on its likelihood and probability, in combination with the impact that may occur within a given time period (e.g., a year). The greater the likelihood (or frequency of occurrence) and the resulting outcome (or consequence/impact), the greater the risk.

texts.label: list_item

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Velocity—In this context, velocity is a consideration of the extent of prior warning of an event and the amount of time between an event's occurrence and the subsequent impact.
texts.text: Velocity—In this context, velocity is a consideration of the extent of prior warning of an event and the amount of time between an event's occurrence and the subsequent impact.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Proximity—This is a term used to indicate the time between an event and the impact (i.e., the greater the velocity, the closer the proximity).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Interdependency—It is important to consider risk not in isolation, but rather in the organizational context and in relationship to other assets and functions. The materialization of several types of risk might affect the enterprise differently depending in part on whether the risk events occur concurrently or sequentially.

The nature of the motivation affects, to some extent, the type of assets at risk (i.e., politically motivated nation states will typically target different assets than criminals seeking financial gain will target, thereby affecting the risk to particular assets).

texts.orig: 2.1.6 Risk Register
texts.text: 2.1.6 Risk Register

texts.label: text
texts.orig: During the process of identifying risk and its components, a risk register should be established. The register should serve as a central repository for all information security risk, including specific threats, vulnerabilities, exposures and assets affected. It should include the asset owner, the risk owner and other stakeholders.
texts.text: During the process of identifying risk and its components, a risk register should be established. The register should serve as a central repository for all information security risk, including specific threats, vulnerabilities, exposures and assets affected. It should include the asset owner, the risk owner and other stakeholders.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As the risk register is a living repository, content within the risk register should be filled out as the assessment process gets underway. Once the identification, analysis, evaluation and risk response efforts have been completed and other pertinent information has been entered into the register, it will serve as an authoritative reference point for all risk management-related activities.

Once the identification, analysis, evaluation and risk response efforts have been completed and other pertinent information has been entered into the register, it will serve as an authoritative reference point for all risk management-related activities.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Risk registers enhance accountability by assigning risk to risk owners and provide a tracking mechanism for ensuring risk has been mitigated according to the agreed action plans and within the agreed timelines. Without a risk register, there is lack of accountability.

texts.text: 2.2 Vulnerability and Control Deficiency Analysis

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The term vulnerability, also referred to as weakness, is often used for a binary condition. Something is vulnerable or it is not vulnerable. In most cases, assets are vulnerable to varying degrees (i.e., a particular control condition represents a high degree of vulnerability, while another control condition represents a lower degree of vulnerability). The extent of exposure must be considered, as it affects the probability that a vulnerability is compromised. These distinctions become critical in the process of prioritizing risk management efforts, when determining the level of risk within a scenario, and also when explaining conclusions and recommendations to management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The NIST Special Publication 800-30 Revision 1: Guide to Conducting Risk Assessments provides a list of vulnerabilities to consider, along with predisposing conditions that may lead to the rapid or unpredictable emergence of new vulnerabilities. Many vulnerabilities are conditions that exist in systems and must be identified before they can be addressed. The purpose of vulnerability identification is to find the problems before they are found by an adversary and exploited, which is why an enterprise should conduct regular vulnerability assessments and penetration tests to identify, validate and classify its vulnerabilities. An assessment of vulnerabilities must consider process and procedural weaknesses along with logical ones. Where vulnerabilities exist, there is potential for risk.

texts.orig: 2.2.1 Security Control Baselines
texts.text: 2.2.1 Security Control Baselines

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Controls are designed as part of the information security risk management framework, which incorporates policies, standards, procedures, practices and organizational structures. It is designed to provide reasonable assurance that business objectives are achieved and the potential impacts of undesired events are sufficiently addressed. The framework must consider people, processes and technology and encompass the physical, technical, contractual and procedural aspects of the enterprise. It must take into account the strategic, programmatic, operational and tactical components of the enterprise to be effective.
texts.text: Controls are designed as part of the information security risk management framework, which incorporates policies, standards, procedures, practices and organizational structures. It is designed to provide reasonable assurance that business objectives are achieved and the potential impacts of undesired events are sufficiently addressed. The framework must consider people, processes and technology and encompass the physical, technical, contractual and procedural aspects of the enterprise. It must take into account the strategic, programmatic, operational and tactical components of the enterprise to be effective.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Safeguards include any practice, procedure, process or other instrumentation that serves to reduce risk through the application of a precautionary measure to protect a business asset. Safeguards are considered proactive controls in that they are applied and used in an attempt to prevent an event from occurring. Some examples of proactive controls or safeguards inclúde employee background checks, intrusion prevention systems (IPSs) and turnstile gates.

Safeguards are considered proactive controls in that they are applied and used in an attempt to prevent an event from occurring. Some examples of proactive controls or safeguards inclúde employee background checks, intrusion prevention systems (IPSs) and turnstile gates.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Countermeasures include practices, procedures, processes or other instrumentation used to respond to an event that has occurred. Countermeasures typically respond to a threat or vulnerability once it has been identified. The implementation and integration of countermeasures can take a variety of forms and can range from modifying architecture or reengineering processes, to reducing or eliminating internal threats to technical vulnerabilities, to creating an employee awareness program to target social engineering and promote early recognition and reporting of security incidents.

However, the information security manager must keep in mind that every enterprise has its own needs and priorities. While NIST, ISO, COBIT and vendors can provide starting points of support for developing controls, specific analysis should always be performed.

texts.orig: Controls suitable for the enterprise must be developed based on a variety of factors—such as culture, ethics, organizational structure, staffing, skills and available supporting infrastructure—in the context of the enterprise's defined risk appetite and tolerance. When defining the risk analysis program, it is important to consider people and processes in addition to technology. The information security manager needs to develop procedural and physical security baselines. This will often present a challenge due to some areas typically being outside the control of the information security department. Appropriate standards approved by the steering committee, as described in Chapter 1, can be the most effective approach to address this issue. Internal audit and regular security reviews can help provide assurance of conformance required by the governing authority.

The information security manager needs to develop procedural and physical security baselines. Appropriate standards approved by the steering committee, as described in Chapter 1, can be the most effective approach to address this issue. Internal audit and regular security reviews can help provide assurance of conformance required by the governing authority.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Implementing baselines for security processes sets the minimum security requirements throughout the enterprise so they are consistent with acceptable risk levels. Different baselines must be established for different security classifications, with more stringent security controls required for the higher classification levels of the more critical or sensitive assets. If the enterprise has not implemented a classification scheme, it will be difficult for the information security manager to develop a rational basis for setting baselines without the risk of overprotecting some resources and underprotecting others.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In order to formulate a baseline of security controls, some measurement of the effectiveness and efficiency of controls is necessary. A baseline is not established on a single test of controls, but on the overall capacity of controls to collectively mitigate risk to acceptable levels.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To set control baselines, security managers can refer to many of the published standards that may be implemented within the enterprise. Based on these standards, a test of the control can be performed multiple times to establish an evaluation of the effectiveness and efficiency of the control required by the standard.
texts.text: To set control baselines, security managers can refer to many of the published standards that may be implemented within the enterprise. Based on these standards, a test of the control can be performed multiple times to establish an evaluation of the effectiveness and efficiency of the control required by the standard.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Setting security baselines for an enterprise has a number of benefits. It standardizes the minimum number of security measures that must be employed throughout the enterprise; this not only results in positive benefits for risk management but also allows operational management according to classification level instead of a Selecting relevant metrics among the numerous available per system or per asset basis. It provides a convenient point of reference to measure changes to security and identify corresponding effects on risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While it is important for information security managers to be aware of industry standard baselines, they must assess the level of security that should be employed in various areas of the enterprise. The commingling of different technologies, data and users/consumers can often introduce new risk and change a secure system or platform into one that has new vulnerabilities. A tailored risk assessment that recognizes these interactions and dependencies will enable the information security manager to determine whether security processes and procedures above the defined baselines are necessary to provide adequate security commensurate with the enterprise's defined levels of acceptable risk. Some enterprises and industries may require higher baselines, such as highly regulated industries. That may also be the case for an enterprise that handles information that is classified as highly critical or sensitive. In both of these cases, the enterprise must have control mechanisms that provide a high level of security commensurate with these requirements.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Security baselines may be modified for various reasons. For example, a vendor may identify a parameter in its software or hardware that must be changed to achieve or maintain the desired protection levels. Another reason for modification could be an outside event that necessitated an increase in the established baselines. For example, a protest or other civil unrest near an enterprise facility might warrant an increase in the baseline for physical security for a period until the threat passed. Other drivers include new or changing laws or regulations, identification of unacceptable risk levels because of new or changing threats, degradation of controls over time, and system changes creating new vulnerabilities.

texts.orig: The information security manager should set up a regular, formal process in which risk assessments are performed at the organizational, system and application levels, including business processes both logical and physical. Ensuring that there are appropriate measurements (metrics) in place to assess the risk and the effectiveness of security measures is part of the information security manager's ongoing responsibility. The effectiveness of security measures or controls should be assessed against control objectives and security baselines. This risk assessment process is important because it focuses the enterprise's security activities on issues that have the greatest likelihood, impact and significance.

Interruption to business operations is a major concern, and preventing it should be a primary focus of risk management. In some cases, incidents will escalate to disasters and fall under the purview of business continuity and disaster recovery. texts.orig: 2.3.3 Risk Management Integration with IT Life Cycle Management Processes
texts.text: 2.3.3 Risk Management Integration with IT Life Cycle Management Processes

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ensuring that risk identification, analysis, evaluation, assessment and response activities are integrated into life cycle processes is an important task for information security management.
texts.text: Ensuring that risk identification, analysis, evaluation, assessment and response activities are integrated into life cycle processes is an important task for information security management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The need to minimize the negative impact on an enterprise and to establish a sound basis for decision making are the fundamental reasons enterprises implement a risk management process for their IT systems. Effective risk management must be fully integrated into the system development life cycle (SDLC). An IT system's SDLC has five phases: initiation, development or acquisition, implementation, operation or maintenance, and disposal. In some cases, an IT system may occupy several of these phases at the same time. However, the risk management methodology is the same, regardless of the SDLC phase for which the assessment is being conducted. Risk management is an iterative process that can be performed during each major phase of the SDLC. See Section 3.6.3 Life Cycle Principles Supporting the Road Map for more information.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Enterprises typically have change management procedures that can provide the information security manager with an approach to implementing risk management processes on an ongoing basis. Because changes to any information resource are likely to introduce new vulnerabilities and change the overall risk equation, it is important that the information security manager be aware of proposed modifications within the environment. With distributed computing having become the norm, changes are made more easily in a dispersed environment by people with limited knowiedge. Enterprises often experience a lack of standardization in their hardware and software environments. Management in many enterprises has therefore instituted more robust change management procedures and, as a consequence, has begun to achieve better control over enterprise information resources. This is a moving target, and enterprises with remote operations are, in some cases, still finding effective change management an elusive goal.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Change management processes may already be established for other business areas and activities. One benefit is that many enterprises now have change management procedures that span the entire enterprise. The information security manager must be aware of these change management activities and ensure that security is properly integrated with business operations so changes are not made without considering the implications to the overall security of the enterprise's information assets. One method of helping to ensure this is for information security management to participate as a member of the change management committee and ensure that all changes are subject to review and approval by security, and that proposed changes meet policy and standards requirements. Any proposed deviations should be identified and documented for further analysis.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While the normal change management focus is on hardware and software changes (testing, sign-offs, etc.) and security impact, the change management process should extend well beyond the system owners and IT population. The change management process must include facilities management with respect to data center infrastructure and any other area that may impact overall information security (e.g., physical access control of sensitive or critical areas).
texts.text: While the normal change management focus is on hardware and software changes (testing, sign-offs, etc.) and security impact, the change management process should extend well beyond the system owners and IT population. The change management process must include facilities management with respect to data center infrastructure and any other area that may impact overall information security (e.g., physical access control of sensitive or critical areas).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The impact of change management on system and facilities maintenance windows must be addressed with facilities personnel (often outsourced) and business continuity management. Often, changes are not documented on a timely basis within these areas. Facilities may not have current single-line drawings and blueprints. Correspondingly, computer infrastructure/configuration management may not have the changes properly documented or updated on a timely basis. Business continuity may lag when relevant updates occur in cycles. Emergency response and business continuity may suffer communications lapses when current and changing processes are not reviewed within facility infrastructure areas.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Facilities personnel often have access to environmental monitoring and control systems (building management system [BMS]/supervisory control and data acquisition [SCADA] systems) for heating, ventilating and air conditioning (HVAC), water and electricity, or even physical access control systems (PACS). These are often programmed for remote computer access, an area that often escapes information security oversight. Physical security and control systems have been designed within the context of their deployment within a closed/controlled environment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: IT systems can also be compromised due to vulnerabilities in the physical security system. Physical security and control systems, because of their importance in the protection of facilities and people, may be part of the enterprise's critical infrastructure. The means of protecting these systems, their system codes and data need to be integrated into the enterprise security classification schemes. Facility service contracts in support of physical and control systems often have emergency response clauses. Those contracts should be reviewed, because they may lack adequate service level agreements or fail to provide sufficient details and accountability for an adequate emergency response. A high-availability application may suffer unforeseen business impacts as a result of facilities failures.

texts.orig: Internal or external parties managing the facilities are sometimes overlooked from a risk management perspective, even though human beings pose the greatest threat to information security. Human beings may be negligent in complying with established processes, ignorant of known threats, willing to engage in collusion or subject to emotional behavior. It is important to include the human factor in assessing the risk associated with critical information assets. Internal parties include operators whose job roles grant them direct physical access to the systems and facilities. External parties include servicing agents (e.g., cleaning or maintenance crew). Possible controls are background screening, employment terms, annual confirmation (via signature) of compliance to code of conducts, or contractual terms in the case of external parties.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is not uncommon for enterprises to leverage or rely on third-party services in a number of different areas, not just IT services. Facility management may be outsourced to a third party, as may certain business activities and processes. The enterprise must ensure that risk acceptance and tolerance levels are not exceeded in areas outsourced to a third party. Risk management needs to be integrated in all phases of third-party management, including identification of requirements, evaluation and selection of suppliers, contracting, and regular review, in addition to onboarding and offboarding.

texts.orig: By integrating risk identification, analysis, assessment and response activities into change management (life cycle processes), the information security manager can ensure that critical information resources are adequately protected. This is a proactive approach, enabling the information security manager to better plan and implement security policies and procedures in alignment with the business goals and objectives of the enterprise. It permits the interjection of information security controls into an activity that holds the greatest potential for degrading existing controls.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Because risk management is a continuous process, the information security manager should view risk management itself as having a continuous life cycle. This life cycle includes assessment, treatment and monitoring phases, as illustrated in figure 2.8. Employing a life cycle-based risk management approach that is integrated with change management limits costs in that a full risk assessment does not have to be performed periodically. Instead, updates may be made to the risk assessment and risk management processes on an incremental basis.

texts.orig: The development of risk scenarios is based on describing a potential risk event and documenting the factors and areas that may be affected by the risk event. Risk events may include system failure, loss of key personnel, theft, network outages, power failures, natural disasters or any other situations that could affect business operations and mission. Each risk scenario should be related to a business objective or impact experienced by the enterprise. The key to developing effective scenarios is to focus on real and relevant potential risk events. Examples are developing a risk scenario based on a radical change in the market for an enterprise's products, a change in government or leadership, or a supply chain failure. Figure 2.10 shows an example of the many inputs that are required to develop risk scenarios.

texts.label: text

texts.orig: 2.3.6 Risk Assessment and Analysis Methodologies
texts.text: 2.3.6 Risk Assessment and Analysis Methodologies

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Numerous risk management models and assessment approaches are available to the information security manager. The approach selected should be determined by the best form, fit and function. The approaches include COBIT, OCTAVE®, NIST 800-39, HB 158-2010, ISO 27005:20018, ISO/IEC 31000, ITIL® and CRAMM. Other approaches—such as Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR), Holistic Approach to Risk Management (HARM), risk factor analysis and value at risk (VAR)—may be more suitable, depending on the enterprise and the specific requirements.
texts.text: Numerous risk management models and assessment approaches are available to the information security manager. The approach selected should be determined by the best form, fit and function. The approaches include COBIT, OCTAVE®, NIST 800-39, HB 158-2010, ISO 27005:20018, ISO/IEC 31000, ITIL® and CRAMM. Other approaches—such as Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR), Holistic Approach to Risk Management (HARM), risk factor analysis and value at risk (VAR)—may be more suitable, depending on the enterprise and the specific requirements.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the COBIT approach, risk scenarios involve the process of identifying risk, followed by analysis. Risk evaluation is the next step to determine whether risk exceeds acceptable levels. These three steps allow the risk assessment to generate a recommendation of the appropriate risk response, or risk treatment. Response (treatment) priorities are based on a cost-benefit and risk-level analysis, with high cost-benefit and high likelihood/high impact taking the highest priority.

texts.orig: Cascading Risk
texts.text: Cascading Risk

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cascading risk can manifest unacceptable impacts as a result of one failure leading to a chain reaction of failures. An example of this occurred on the East Coast of the United States when a failure at a small power utility in the Midwest caused a cascade of failures across the power grid, ultimately encompassing most of the northeastern quarter of the United States. Similarly, to the extent that portions of the enterprise's IT and other operations have closely coupled dependencies, the information security manager must consider how any particular failures or combinations of failures will affect dependent systems.

texts.orig: Probabilistic Risk Assessment
texts.text: Probabilistic Risk Assessment

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) has emerged as an increasingly popular analysis tool, especially during the last decade. PRA is a systematic and comprehensive methodology to evaluate risk associated with every life cycle aspect of a complex engineered technological entity, from concept definition through design, construction and operation, and up to removal from service. Developed for use by the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the nuclear power industry, the approach is complex and time-consuming, but it may see increasing application in cases that require high network security.
texts.text: Probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) has emerged as an increasingly popular analysis tool, especially during the last decade. PRA is a systematic and comprehensive methodology to evaluate risk associated with every life cycle aspect of a complex engineered technological entity, from concept definition through design, construction and operation, and up to removal from service. Developed for use by the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the nuclear power industry, the approach is complex and time-consuming, but it may see increasing application in cases that require high network security.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The approach aims to answer three questions:
texts.text: The approach aims to answer three questions:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: What can go wrong?
texts.text: What can go wrong?

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: How likely is it?
texts.text: How likely is it?

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: What are the consequences?
texts.text: What are the consequences?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The answers are based on a thorough deconstruction of all the elements at risk in a particular set of circumstances, followed by systematically identifying, modeling and quantifying scenarios that can lead to adverse consequences based on probability and statistical theory, reliability engineering, decision theory and other information. Elements that go into assessing a possible chain of events include hardware and software failure, human actions, control failures and other possible interactions that can lead to serious consequences.

Elements that go into assessing a possible chain of events include hardware and software failure, human actions, control failures and other possible interactions that can lead to serious consequences.

texts.orig: 2.3.8 Risk Analysis
texts.text: 2.3.8 Risk Analysis

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Risk analysis is the phase in which potential probability and resulting outcomes are calculated and determined. This phase includes determining threat actor capabilities and motivations, the effectiveness of existing controls, and the extent to which they may influence a particular identified risk.
texts.text: Risk analysis is the phase in which potential probability and resulting outcomes are calculated and determined. This phase includes determining threat actor capabilities and motivations, the effectiveness of existing controls, and the extent to which they may influence a particular identified risk.

texts.label: text

texts.text: Risk analysis involves:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Thorough examination of the risk sources (threats and vulnerabilities) determined in the risk identification phase
texts.text: Thorough examination of the risk sources (threats and vulnerabilities) determined in the risk identification phase

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: The extent to which information assets have exposure to potential threats and the effect on likelihood
texts.text: The extent to which information assets have exposure to potential threats and the effect on likelihood

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: The potential negative consequences (impact) if the assets are successfully attacked
texts.text: The potential negative consequences (impact) if the assets are successfully attacked

texts.label: list_item

texts.text: The likelihood that those consequences may occur and the factors that affect them

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Gap Analysis
texts.text: Gap Analysis

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Gap analysis in the context of risk management refers to determining the gap between existing controls and control objectives. Control objectives based on acceptable risk should have been defined as an outcome of developing an information security governance and management strategy as discussed in Chapter 1.
texts.text: Gap analysis in the context of risk management refers to determining the gap between existing controls and control objectives. Control objectives based on acceptable risk should have been defined as an outcome of developing an information security governance and management strategy as discussed in Chapter 1.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Control objectives should lead to controls that result in residual risk falling into acceptable levels, ensuring that the established information security baseline is maintained.
texts.text: Control objectives should lead to controls that result in residual risk falling into acceptable levels, ensuring that the established information security baseline is maintained.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Control objectives may change as a part of risk management activities as exposures, business objectives, operations, contractual obligations or regulations change, potentially creating a gap between the existing control and its revised objectives. Periodically analyzing the gap between controls and their objectives should be a standard practice. This is normally accomplished as a part of the process of controls testing for effectiveness. To the extent that effectiveness of controls fails to meet the control objective and achieve acceptable risk, the controls may need to be modified, redesigned or supplemented with additional control activities. For more information on the relationship between controls and control objectives, see Chapter 3.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In semi-quantitative analysis, the objective is to define a set of agreed-upon ranged values that are wide enough to allow risk to be estimated consistently. The goal is to provide sufficient accuracy to allow for the understanding, comparison and prioritization of risk. Qualitative terms are usually subjective; the ability to define and map them to quantitative values normalizes basic definitions used to forecast potential outcomes.

texts.orig: ALE is the annual expected financial loss to an asset, resulting from one specific threat. ALE adds the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) to the equation with the result that multiple occurrences will result in greater potential losses. ALE is usually expressed as: ALE = SLE × ARO. The result is that the greater the asset value, coupled with a greater probability and greater magnitude of impact, the greater the potential risk of loss.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: ARO is the number of times a threat on a single asset is estimated to occur. The higher the risk associated with the threat, the higher the ARO. For example, if insurance data suggest that a serious fire is likely to occur once in 25 years, then the annualized rate of occurrence is 1/25 = 0.04.

texts.orig: 2.3.9 Risk Evaluation
texts.text: 2.3.9 Risk Evaluation

texts.label: text
texts.orig: During the risk evaluation phase, decisions are made concerning how the enterprise responds to and prioritizes risk, based on the foregoing analysis, with allowances made for the likely margin of error, which may be considerable if reliable data are not available. This is done in the context of the enterprise's defined risk appetite, tolerance criteria and capacity—establishing a method to advise a reasonable and appropriate risk response.

This is done in the context of the enterprise's defined risk appetite, tolerance criteria and capacity—establishing a method to advise a reasonable and appropriate risk response.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If the risk meets the acceptable risk criteria, the treatment option is likely to be acceptance. If the risk exceeds the acceptable level and is not within the tolerance variance, then treatment will most likely be some form of mitigation. The mitigation options include modification or addition of controls or business process reengineering that would render a process less risky. A system redesign can serve to reduce technical risk (e.g., eliminating a single point of system failure), or risk transfer (or sharing) might be the most cost-effective option. If there are no cost-effective options for mitigating excessive risk, management may decide that the activity is not worth the risk, or it may decide to accept the risk if the benefits are sufficiently high.

texts.orig: 2.3.10 Risk Ranking
texts.text: 2.3.10 Risk Ranking

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The risk practitioner uses the results of risk assessment to place risk in an order that can be used to help the risk owner direct the risk response efforts. Risk ranking is derived from a combination of all the components of risk, including the recognition of the threats and the characteristics and capabilities of a threat source, the severity of a vulnerability, the likelihood of occurrence when considering effectiveness of controls, control risk, and the impact to the enterprise should the risk be realized. Taken together, these indicate the level of risk associated with a threat.

texts.orig: A key to understanding the appropriate risk response is to understand the enterprise's desired state of security, as discussed in Chapter 1. A major input into defining the desired state is the enterprise's defined risk appetite, tolerance criteria and capacity—that is, what management considers acceptable risk, tolerable deviations from acceptable risk levels, and total amount of risk that does not jeopardize the enterprise's viability to operate. This is another critical step, since defined acceptable risk translates into the control objectives or other risk mitigation measures employed and the criteria by which risk can be evaluated for acceptability. The defining of control objectives is instrumental in determining the type, nature and extent of controls and countermeasures the enterprise employs to manage risk. Figure 2.18 presents the relationship between risk, control measures and the cost of controls.

texts.orig: The definition of some risk—and ultimately what the enterprise defines as being acceptable—can be quantified by using the business continuity approach of developing recovery time objectives (RTOs). Using a summary approach to determining RTOs may provide adequate input for strategy development. This can be an informal determination by business process owners of the amount of time critical systems can be inoperative without serious business consequences. This provides the basis for approximating costs of achieving recovery. If costs are considered too high, iteration of the process will arrive at an acceptable recovery time at an acceptable cost. This may be considered the acceptable risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Acceptable risk can also be approximated by examining the amount of business interruption insurance the enterprise carries, the amount of the deductible and its cost (i.e., annual premiums). For example, if the enterprise has US $1 million of insurance with a $10,000 deductible at an annual cost of $50,000, the argument can be made that it is reasonable to spend up to $50,000 in control activities to reduce a $1 million risk to an acceptable risk level of $10,000 (i.e., the residual risk).

texts.orig: For example, risk may exist because of certain practices that are not necessary or useful to the enterprise or are detrimental to its operation. This could include practices that might be considered discriminatory or contrary to law, posing the risk of a lawsuit. Such practices, when examined, may have resulted from outmoded attitudes or approaches that can be efficiently changed at a lower cost, resulting in elimination or mitigation of the risk. In other cases, it may be possible to reengineer certain processes or provide better architectures to reduce inherent risk. In other words, the approach to addressing or treating specific risk has a significant impact on costs.

texts.orig: 2.4.1 Determining Risk Capacity and Acceptable Risk (Risk Appetite)
texts.text: 2.4.1 Determining Risk Capacity and Acceptable Risk (Risk Appetite)

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Every enterprise has a particular risk capacity, defined as the objective amount of loss an enterprise can tolerate without its continued existence being threatened. Subject to the absolute maximum imposed by this risk capacity, the owners or board of directors of an enterprise set the risk appetite for the enterprise. Risk appetite is defined as the amount of risk, on a broad basis, that an entity is willing to accept in pursuit of its mission. In some cases, the board of directors may delegate setting the risk appetite to senior management as part of strategic planning.

Subject to the absolute maximum imposed by this risk capacity, the owners or board of directors of an enterprise set the risk appetite for the enterprise. Risk appetite is defined as the amount of risk, on a broad basis, that an entity is willing to accept in pursuit of its mission. In some cases, the board of directors may delegate setting the risk appetite to senior management as part of strategic planning.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Acceptable risk determination or risk appetite and the criteria for assessment are essential to virtually all aspects of information security and most other aspects of organizational activities. Risk appetite will determine many aspects of strategy including control objectives, control implementation, baseline security, cost-benefit calculations, risk management options, severity criteria determinations, required incident response capabilities, insurance requirements and feasibility assessments, among others.

texts.orig: Risk acceptance generally should not exceed the risk appetite of the enterprise, but it must not exceed the risk capacity (which would threaten the continued existence of the enterprise). Risk tolerance levels are risk appetite deviations that are not desirable but are known to be sufficiently below the risk capacity that acceptance of risk is still possible when there is compelling business need and other options are too costly. Risk tolerance may be defined using IT process metrics or adherence to defined IT procedures and policies, which are a translation of the IT goals that need to be achieved. Like risk appetite, risk tolerance is defined at the enterprise level and reflected in the policies created by senior management. Exceptions can be tolerated at lower levels of the enterprise as long as the overall exposure does not exceed the risk appetite at the enterprise level.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One thing to keep in mind is that while the information security manager is bound to recommend one of the four risk responses listed above, the enterprise may choose to ignore the risk, which can be dangerous. The distinction between ignoring and accepting risk is that acceptance means understanding the likelihood, probability and consequences and making an informed decision to accept the risk under the circumstances. Ignoring a risk may lead to a serious underestimation of both the likelihood and possible magnitude of the impact, with severe or disastrous consequences. Accordingly, this is an inadvisable course of action. The only time it may be prudent to ignore an identified risk is when the impact is so great and rare that there is no possibility of addressing it (e.g., a comet strike).

texts.orig: Mitigate the Risk
texts.text: Mitigate the Risk

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Risk can be mitigated in a variety of ways, such as through implementing or improving security controls, instituting countermeasures, or modifying or eliminating risky processes. Preventive controls can directly address the risk, or it may be possible to reduce exposure, thereby reducing risk. In some cases, risk can be reduced through appropriate countermeasures that reduce or eliminate the probability of a threat.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Accept the Risk
texts.text: Accept the Risk

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A defined risk may be accepted in a variety of circumstances. If a risk has been identified as below the defined risk acceptance levels (both the defined risk appetite and risk tolerance criteria), the risk should be accepted and monitored moving forward. There are a few limited cases in which it may not be feasible to effectively mitigate a risk for which there is low likelihood of realization or low potential impact. This effectively results in increasing the risk acceptance level for a specific risk for a defined duration or financial amount. However, it is not intended to be, nor should it be treated as, the perpetual acceptance of that risk.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.4.4 Inherent and Residual Risk
texts.text: 2.4.4 Inherent and Residual Risk

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The risk level or exposure without taking into account the actions that management has taken or might take (e.g., implementing controls) is called inherent risk. The risk that remains after controls have been implemented is called residual risk. Risk can never be eliminated, as a certain level of residual risk always remains even with the application of appropriate controls. It should be noted that reducing one risk inevitably introduces another risk, hopefully of a lesser nature. For example, requiring dual control to access sensitive information introduces the risk that two individuals collude to provide unauthorized access.
texts.text: The risk level or exposure without taking into account the actions that management has taken or might take (e.g., implementing controls) is called inherent risk. The risk that remains after controls have been implemented is called residual risk. Risk can never be eliminated, as a certain level of residual risk always remains even with the application of appropriate controls. It should be noted that reducing one risk inevitably introduces another risk, hopefully of a lesser nature. For example, requiring dual control to access sensitive information introduces the risk that two individuals collude to provide unauthorized access.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The objective is to ensure that residual risk is equal to the enterprise's criteria for acceptable risk or meets risk tolerance criteria. Risk tolerance is defined as the allowable deviation from acceptable risk and is usually described as a percentage (e.g., plus or minus 10 percent) or range (e.g., a project exceeding planned duration by four weeks). Acceptable residual risk should be the outcome of meeting the defined control objectives and be equivalent to the defined security baselines for the enterprise.
texts.text: The objective is to ensure that residual risk is equal to the enterprise's criteria for acceptable risk or meets risk tolerance criteria. Risk tolerance is defined as the allowable deviation from acceptable risk and is usually described as a percentage (e.g., plus or minus 10 percent) or range (e.g., a project exceeding planned duration by four weeks). Acceptable residual risk should be the outcome of meeting the defined control objectives and be equivalent to the defined security baselines for the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Residual risk reported through a subsequent risk assessment can be used by management to identify areas in which more control is required to further mitigate risk. Acceptable levels of risk are established as part of an information security strategy, as described in Chapter 1. If a strategy is not developed, management must determine the acceptable risk levels, usually in terms of allowable potential impacts. Residual risk in excess of the acceptable level should be further treated with the option of additional mitigation through implementing more stringent controls. Risk below the acceptable level should be evaluated to determine whether the controls being applied are still warranted, and whether a cost savings can be achieved by removing or modifying them. Final acceptance of residual risk takes into account:

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.4.7 Legal and Regulatory Requirements
texts.text: 2.4.7 Legal and Regulatory Requirements

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Legal and regulatory requirements must be considered in terms of risk and impact. This is necessary for senior management to determine the appropriate level of compliance and priority. Regulations must first be evaluated by legal/general counsel to determine the exposure the enterprise is subject to by the regulation and the present level at which the enterprise can demonstrate compliance. If it is found that the enterprise is noncompliant, then the regulations must be evaluated to determine the level of risk they pose to the enterprise. The enterprise must take into consideration the level of enforcement and its relative position in relation to its peers, because enforcement actions are usually initiated against those that are least compliant. The potential impact of full compliance, partial compliance and noncompliance, in both direct financial and reputational terms, must be evaluated as well. These evaluations provide the basis for senior management to determine the nature and extent of compliance activities appropriate for the enterprise. The information security manager must be aware that senior management may decide that risking sanctions is less costly than achieving compliance, or that because enforcement is limited, or even nonexistent, compliance is not warranted. This is a management decision that should be based on risk and impact.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When controls are planned, an enterprise should consider the costs and benefits. If the costs of specific controls (control overhead) exceed the benefits of mitigating a given risk, the enterprise may choose to accept the risk rather than incur the cost of mitigation.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cost-benefit analysis helps provide a financial view of risk and helps determine the cost of protecting what is important. However, cost-benefit analysis is also about making smart choices based on potential risk mitigation costs versus potential losses. Both concepts tie directly back to good governance practices.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.5 Risk and Control Ownership
texts.text: 2.5 Risk and Control Ownership

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Who owns the risk? This is a commonly asked question and the answer is, it depends. From a strategic standpoint, all risk ultimately is owned by senior management. As a matter of practicality and from an operational standpoint, ownership is delegated to the individuals who have the authority and responsibility for managing risk in accordance with the criteria established by the governing body within their respective business areas, driving ownership of both risk and controls to the relevant business process owner (i.e., the business).

As a matter of practicality and from an operational standpoint, ownership is delegated to the individuals who have the authority and responsibility for managing risk in accordance with the criteria established by the governing body within their respective business areas, driving ownership of both risk and controls to the relevant business process owner (i.e., the business).

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.5.1 Risk Ownership and Accountability
texts.text: 2.5.1 Risk Ownership and Accountability

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Risk requires ownership and accountability. After a risk has been identified, analyzed and evaluated, a manager or senior official within the enterprise must be identified as its owner. A risk owner is accountable for accepting risk based on the organizational risk appetite and tolerance criteria, and should be someone with the capability (e.g., budget, authority, resources) to select the appropriate risk response based on analyses and guidance provided by the information security manager. This accountability extends to approving controls when mitigation is the chosen risk response. Types of controls are examined in more detail in Chapter 3. However, the concept is to create a direct link, so that all risk is addressed through appropriate treatment and all controls are justified by the risk that mandates their existence. Figure 2.21 illustrates the relationship between risk and control.

texts.orig: 2.5.2 Risk Owner
texts.text: 2.5.2 Risk Owner

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The term risk owner can be defined as the person to whom the enterprise has granted the authority and accountability for making risk-based decisions and who owns the loss associated with a realized risk scenario. From a strategic aspect, senior management (e.g., chief executive officer, president, founder) is the risk owner who is ultimately accountable for risk response for the entirety of the enterprise. From an operational and management perspective, directors, vice presidents, managers, etc., are the individuals who have the authority and responsibility, and should be held accountable, for making decisions relating to risk as a part of routine operations.

texts.orig: 2.5.3 Control Owner
texts.text: 2.5.3 Control Owner

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Control owner, like its counterpart risk owner, is a term that often gets confused. The control owner is the individual to whom the enterprise has granted the authority and accountability for making control-related decisions. The control owner and the risk owner are normally the same individual, as any modifications to or removal of a control will impact the risk being treated, potentially leading to the risk exceeding the defined risk appetite.

The control owner and the risk owner are normally the same individual, as any modifications to or removal of a control will impact the risk being treated, potentially leading to the risk exceeding the defined risk appetite.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Just as with risk ownership, control ownership falls to individuals within the enterprise who have the authority to make decisions related to the controls and who will be held accountable for how risk is managed. IT staff may serve as the custodians/stewards of the controls; however, it is ultimately the business unit that bears accountability if a control should be ineffective in properly treating risk.

texts.orig: 2.6 Risk Monitoring and Reporting
texts.text: 2.6 Risk Monitoring and Reporting

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Implementing an effective risk management program requires regular monitoring and effective communication. Monitoring the effectiveness of controls is an ongoing effort required to manage risk. Communication channels must be established both for reporting and disseminating information relevant to managing risk and for providing the information security manager with information about risk-related activities throughout the enterprise, which includes reporting significant changes in risk and training in awareness.
