Communication channels must be established both for reporting and disseminating information relevant to managing risk and for providing the information security manager with information about risk-related activities throughout the enterprise, which includes reporting significant changes in risk and training in awareness.

Figure 2.22 shows a risk report format from COBIT that can serve as a standard approach for communicating risk status.

texts.orig: 2.6.2 Key Risk Indicators
texts.text: 2.6.2 Key Risk Indicators

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One approach seeing increasing use is to report and monitor risk through the use of key risk indicators (KRIs). KRIs can be defined as measures that indicate when an enterprise is subject to risk that exceeds a defined risk level. Typically, these indicators emerge from trends in factors known to increase risk and are generally developed based on experience. They can be as diverse as increasing absenteeism or turnover in key employees or rising levels of security events or incidents.

KRIs can be defined as measures that indicate when an enterprise is subject to risk that exceeds a defined risk level. Typically, these indicators emerge from trends in factors known to increase risk and are generally developed based on experience. They can be as diverse as increasing absenteeism or turnover in key employees or rising levels of security events or incidents.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: KRIs can provide early warnings on possible issues or areas that pose particular risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A variety of risk indicators can be developed for various parts of an enterprise as a means of ongoing monitoring. In addition to experience, selection of KRIs can be based on sources such as industry benchmarks, external threatreporting services, or any other factor that can be monitored that indicates changes in risk to the enterprise.

texts.text: 2.6.3 Reporting Changes in Risk

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As changes occur in an enterprise, the risk assessment must be updated to ensure its continued accuracy. Reporting changes to the appropriate levels of management (e.g., risk/control owners) at the proper time is a primary responsibility of the information security manager. The information security manager should have periodic meetings with the appropriate, relevant stakeholders to present a risk status and with senior management on the enterprise's overall risk profile, including changes in risk level and the status of any open (untreated) risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In addition, the security program should include a process in which a significant security breach or security event will trigger a report to senior management and a reassessment of risk and applicable controls because all security events or incidents are the result of the failure of, or lack of, controls. The information security manager should have defined processes for evaluating security events based on impact to the enterprise. This evaluation may warrant a special report to inform upper management of the event, the impact, and the steps being taken to mitigate the risk. texts.orig: Risk Awareness
texts.text: Risk Awareness

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Awareness is a powerful tool in creating the culture, shaping ethics and influencing the behavior of the members of an enterprise. The risk and security awareness program should include communication of risk and security information, periodic testing as a metric for awareness, and a channel for staff to report risk and security issues. The staff and operational teams of an enterprise are often the first to be aware of any problems or abnormal activities. Through awareness programs, it is possible to develop a team approach to risk management that enables every member of an enterprise to identify and report on risk and work to defend systems and networks from attacks. Each member of the team can help identify vulnerabilities, suspicious activity and possible attacks. This may enable a faster response and better containment of a risk when an attack happens. Risk awareness acknowledges that risk is an integral part of the business. Because not all risk can be avoided or eliminated, it aims to ensure that:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A risk awareness program creates an understanding of overall risk, risk factors and the various types of risk that an enterprise faces. An awareness program should be tailored to the needs of the individual groups within an enterprise and deliver content suitable for each group. The program should not disclose vulnerabilities or ongoing investigations unless the problem has already been addressed. Using examples and descriptions of the types of attacks and compromises that other enterprises have experienced can reinforce the need for diligence and caution when addressing risk.

An awareness program should be tailored to the needs of the individual groups within an enterprise and deliver content suitable for each group. The program should not disclose vulnerabilities or ongoing investigations unless the problem has already been addressed. Using examples and descriptions of the types of attacks and compromises that other enterprises have experienced can reinforce the need for diligence and caution when addressing risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Awareness education and training can mitigate some of the most significant weaknesses contributing to organizational risk and achieve the most cost-effective improvements in security and risk management. Awareness can generally be achieved by educating an enterprise's staff in required procedures and policy compliance, and ensuring that staff can identify and understand the risk that threatens the enterprise. Training must effectively communicate the risk and its potential impact so staff can understand the justification for the seemingly inconvenient extra steps that risk mitigation and security controls often require.

Procedural and technical controls can be complex, and it is essential to provide training as needed to ensure that staff understands the procedures and can correctly perform the required steps.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Awareness of information security architecture, policies, standards and procedures by all personnel is essential to achieving effective risk management. Employees cannot be expected to comply with policies or standards they are not aware of or follow procedures they do not understand. The information security manager should use a standardized approach, such as short computer- or paper-based quizzes, to gauge awareness levels. Periodic use of a standardized testing approach provides metrics for awareness trends and training effectiveness. Further training needs can be determined by a skills assessment or through testing. Indicators for additional training requirements can come from various sources, such as tracking help desk activity, operational errors, security events and audits.

texts.orig: 2.6.5 Documentation
texts.text: 2.6.5 Documentation

texts.label: text

texts.orig: Case Study
texts.text: Case Study

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A major retailer was compromised, resulting in the loss of about 45 million credit and debit card records. Estimates of the ultimate total costs to the retailer were up to US $18 billion, including costs incurred due to banks having to replace the cards and cover the resultant fraudulent charges. The total included the possible costs of lawsuits, governmental sanctions and fines levied by the major credit card organization for failure to be PCI-compliant. The retailer suffered a 46 percent decrease in holiday sales when the breach was made public.
texts.text: A major retailer was compromised, resulting in the loss of about 45 million credit and debit card records. Estimates of the ultimate total costs to the retailer were up to US $18 billion, including costs incurred due to banks having to replace the cards and cover the resultant fraudulent charges. The total included the possible costs of lawsuits, governmental sanctions and fines levied by the major credit card organization for failure to be PCI-compliant. The retailer suffered a 46 percent decrease in holiday sales when the breach was made public.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Upon analysis of the incident, it was discovered that the breach was facilitated initially by a phishing email to one of the retailer's service providers—a HVAC company. The retailer had a service provider and vendor portal to facilitate purchasing and billing. Once the hackers gained access to the service company, they used the retailer's portal to gain access to the retailer's network. Although the portal was in a segmented portion of the network, the intruders managed to bridge the segment and gain access to the internal network. From there, they gained access to the point-of-sale (POS) system. They were able to install malware on the POS terminals that captured credit and debit card transactions because the POS traffic was in cleartext to avoid the system overhead associated with encryption.
texts.text: Upon analysis of the incident, it was discovered that the breach was facilitated initially by a phishing email to one of the retailer's service providers—a HVAC company. The retailer had a service provider and vendor portal to facilitate purchasing and billing. Once the hackers gained access to the service company, they used the retailer's portal to gain access to the retailer's network. Although the portal was in a segmented portion of the network, the intruders managed to bridge the segment and gain access to the internal network. From there, they gained access to the point-of-sale (POS) system. They were able to install malware on the POS terminals that captured credit and debit card transactions because the POS traffic was in cleartext to avoid the system overhead associated with encryption.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The unencrypted customer information intercepted was stored on the compromised retailer's server and then subsequently exfiltrated to a series of Internet service providers before finally being sent to overseas in an effort to hide the trail. To mask the exfiltration, the data were sent only during normal business hours. Analysis discovered that the exfiltration did not start until several weeks after the malware had been installed.
texts.text: The unencrypted customer information intercepted was stored on the compromised retailer's server and then subsequently exfiltrated to a series of Internet service providers before finally being sent to overseas in an effort to hide the trail. To mask the exfiltration, the data were sent only during normal business hours. Analysis discovered that the exfiltration did not start until several weeks after the malware had been installed.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The retailer had previously contracted with FireEye to monitor its systems for intrusions and malware. Almost immediately, FireEye sent several alerts to the retailer's security department indicating which of the servers were compromised as per the agreement with the retailer. No immediate action was taken by the security group. No action was taken until several weeks later when the retailer received notification from a government agency that it had been compromised.

texts.orig: CISM exam questions are developed with the intent of measuring and testing practical knowledge in information security management. All questions are multiple choice and are designed for one best answer. Every CISM question has a stem (question) and four options (answer choices). The candidate is asked to choose the correct or best answer from the options. The stem may be in the form of a question or incomplete statement. Many times, a CISM examination question will require the candidate to choose the most likely or best answer.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 1. A. Placing an intrusion detection system (IDS) on the Internet side of the firewall is not usually advised (except to assess the traffic hitting the firewall) because the system will generate alerts on all malicious traffic—even though most traffic will be stopped by the firewall and never reach the internal network.
texts.text: A. Placing an intrusion detection system (IDS) on the Internet side of the firewall is not usually advised (except to assess the traffic hitting the firewall) because the system will generate alerts on all malicious traffic—even though most traffic will be stopped by the firewall and never reach the internal network.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. Because firewalls should be installed on hardened servers with minimal services enabled, it would be inappropriate to install an IDS on the same physical device.
texts.text: Because firewalls should be installed on hardened servers with minimal services enabled, it would be inappropriate to install an IDS on the same physical device.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. An IDS should be placed on a screened subnet, which is a demilitarized zone.
texts.text: An IDS should be placed on a screened subnet, which is a demilitarized zone.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. If placing it on the external router were feasible, it would not be advised (except to assess the traffic hitting the firewall) because the system will generate alerts on all malicious traffic—even though most traffic will be stopped by the firewall and never reach the internal network.
texts.text: If placing it on the external router were feasible, it would not be advised (except to assess the traffic hitting the firewall) because the system will generate alerts on all malicious traffic—even though most traffic will be stopped by the firewall and never reach the internal network.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 2. A. Password resets may or may not have anything to do with awareness levels.
texts.text: A. Password resets may or may not have anything to do with awareness levels.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. Reported incidents will provide an indicator of the awareness level of staff. An increase in reported incidents could indicate that the staff is paying more attention to security.
texts.text: Reported incidents will provide an indicator of the awareness level of staff. An increase in reported incidents could indicate that the staff is paying more attention to security.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. The number of incidents resolved may not correlate to staff awareness.
texts.text: The number of incidents resolved may not correlate to staff awareness.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. Access rule violations may or may not have anything to do with awareness levels.
texts.text: Access rule violations may or may not have anything to do with awareness levels.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 3. A. Security monitoring must focus on business-critical information to remain effectively usable by and credible to business users.
texts.text: A. Security monitoring must focus on business-critical information to remain effectively usable by and credible to business users.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. Control risk is the possibility that controls would not detect an incident or error condition and, therefore, is not a correct answer because monitoring would not directly assist in managing this risk.
texts.text: Control risk is the possibility that controls would not detect an incident or error condition and, therefore, is not a correct answer because monitoring would not directly assist in managing this risk.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. Network intrusions are not the only focus of monitoring mechanisms.
texts.text: Network intrusions are not the only focus of monitoring mechanisms.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. Although ideally all security violations should be recorded, this is only one objective of security monitoring.
texts.text: Although ideally all security violations should be recorded, this is only one objective of security monitoring.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 4. A. Right to terminate is usually a part of the service level agreement (SLA) that can be invoked on failure of the outsourcer to meet the terms of the SLA.
texts.text: A. Right to terminate is usually a part of the service level agreement (SLA) that can be invoked on failure of the outsourcer to meet the terms of the SLA.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. The element of limitations of liability is also typically covered as a part of the SLA.
texts.text: The element of limitations of liability is also typically covered as a part of the SLA.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. SLAs provide metrics to which outsourcing firms can be held accountable and will typically cover the other choices as well. This is the most encompassing answer.
texts.text: SLAs provide metrics to which outsourcing firms can be held accountable and will typically cover the other choices as well. This is the most encompassing answer.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. Financial penalties are covered by the SLA in the event of failure of performance as specified in the SLA.
texts.text: Financial penalties are covered by the SLA in the event of failure of performance as specified in the SLA.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: A. Patch management is a preventive control in that it corrects discovered weaknesses by applying a patch to the original program code that eliminates the weakness preventing exploitation.
texts.text: Patch management is a preventive control in that it corrects discovered weaknesses by applying a patch to the original program code that eliminates the weakness preventing exploitation.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. Change management controls the process of introducing changes to systems that may introduce new vulnerabilities.
texts.text: Change management controls the process of introducing changes to systems that may introduce new vulnerabilities.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. Security baselines provide minimum recommended settings to provide a consistent minimum level of security across the enterprise.
texts.text: Security baselines provide minimum recommended settings to provide a consistent minimum level of security across the enterprise.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. Configuration management ensures that incorrect configuration does not result in increased risk and controls the updates to the production environment.
texts.text: Configuration management ensures that incorrect configuration does not result in increased risk and controls the updates to the production environment.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 6. A. Baseline security standards may require access controls, but alone do not prevent unauthorized access.
texts.text: A. Baseline security standards may require access controls, but alone do not prevent unauthorized access.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: B. Violation logs are detective and do not prevent unauthorized access.
texts.text: Violation logs are detective and do not prevent unauthorized access.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: C. Role-based access control helps ensure that users have access only to files and systems appropriate for their job role and is a preventive control.
texts.text: Role-based access control helps ensure that users have access only to files and systems appropriate for their job role and is a preventive control.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: D. Background checks are not a preventive control although they may be predictive based on past events.
texts.text: Background checks are not a preventive control although they may be predictive based on past events.

texts.text: Patching is more related to system hardening and typically a part of maintenance activities.

texts.text: C. Reliance on managers to promptly send in termination notices cannot always be counted on and by itself does not ensure access termination.

texts.orig: Part A: Information Security Program Development
texts.text: Part A: Information Security Program Development

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An information security program encompasses all the activities and resources that collectively provide information security services to an enterprise. The program is the project plan to implement and establish ongoing management of the information security strategy as mentioned in Chapter 1. Primary program activities include design, development and integration of enterprise-wide controls related to information security, along with the ongoing administration and management of these controls. Controls can range from simple policies and processes to highly complex technology solutions. Depending on the size and nature of the enterprise, these activities can be executed by a single individual or a chief information security officer (CISO) managing a large staff with diverse skills. While information security program development has clear goals and provides a road map for large enterprises, it is not as easy and smooth for small and medium scale enterprises (SMEs) because the business needs vary in the short and near term. Hence, the security program needs to be more flexible concerning business needs for SMEs.

texts.orig: 3.1 Information Security Program Overview
texts.text: 3.1 Information Security Program Overview

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Successful security program management is not significantly different from management of any other organizational activity. The primary difference is that, despite increased visibility, information security remains a somewhat ill-defined and frequently misunderstood discipline.
texts.text: Successful security program management is not significantly different from management of any other organizational activity. The primary difference is that, despite increased visibility, information security remains a somewhat ill-defined and frequently misunderstood discipline.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Often, information security managers have a technical background. Many did not embark on a management career; rather, they were technologists who found themselves increasingly faced with management functions and responsibilities. In many cases, the shift of information security toward a broader management role is driven by the increased desire of a business to understand why specific security controls are required, and how the business will benefit specifically from them. In short, senior management wants to understand the specific risk the information security program is addressing and why the controls it mandates are a sound investment and actually benefit the business. As a result, many information security professionals have had to expand their view beyond technology and develop a greater understanding of the business activities they are seeking to protect.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The dual trends of growing security organizations and increased pressure from the business to ensure that the security program is aligned with the business objectives have combined to broaden the body of knowledge security managers must master. An extensive range of business knowledge and understanding must now be added to the base of information security knowledge that all security professionals should possess. This presents an opportunity for the information security manager to establish an effective bridge between the organizational business needs and the needs of the information technology and security teams. Implementing and executing a program that manages information risk in a cost-effective manner—at the same time enabling business initiatives while protecting organizational interests—supports enterprise awareness and improvement.

texts.text: 3.1.1 Information Security Management Trends

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In an increasing number of enterprises, the information security manager is a member of senior leadership, designated as vice president of security, CISO or chief security officer (CSO), as detailed in Section 1.4.1 Roles and Responsibilities. Also, a number of security functions may report to an independent corporate-level security organization. These functions include physical and information security, IT security, compliance, privacy, business continuity planning/disaster recovery and security architecture. In some large multinational enterprises, many or all these functions are currently included under a senior corporate risk manager or chief risk officer (CRO). Irrespective of the reporting structure of the CISO or information security manager, the critical requirement is to ensure the board of directors or the top decision-making board of the enterprise gets periodic updates from the security organization. Without such updates, business leadership of the enterprise has insufficient visibility of the information security posture.

texts.text: 3.1.3 Importance of the Information Security Program

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security program management is an ongoing requirement that serves to protect information assets, satisfy regulatory obligations, lead appropriate response to incidents, and minimize potential legal and liability exposures.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A well-executed security program is one that is effectively designed, implemented, managed and monitored, transforming strategy into actuality. While providing the capabilities to meet security objectives, the program also accommodates the inevitable changes in security requirements and risk landscape. The program takes advantage of security expertise, tools and techniques that are available in the infrastructure and draws upon partnerships (such as with external vendors and service providers) to support ongoing requirements. The well-designed security program increases the likelihood that the efforts are well integrated, decreasing costs of maintenance and administration while providing a consistent level of security across the enterprise.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Risk Management
texts.text: Risk Management

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Managing the risk to information assets is a primary responsibility of the information security manager and provides the foundation and rationale for virtually all information security activities. Risk analysis must be based on business requirements and an understanding of the enterprise's processes, culture and technology. To effectively manage risk, the information security manager must develop a comprehensive understanding of threats the enterprise faces, its vulnerabilities, its risk profile and the level of risk that management determines is acceptable. The potential impacts of threats that can materialize must be evaluated and used to establish treatment priorities. Risk must be managed to a level that is acceptable to the enterprise. However, the risk landscape is always changing, and new risk will inevitably arise during program development and administration. It is important that a continuous process of risk management be maintained during program development, implementation and evolution.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An information security manager is rarely faced with a situation in which no information security activity is present in an enterprise. Therefore, only rarely will the information security program need to be built from scratch. More often, developing the information security program will be a process of comparing the existing program to what is required to reach the desired information security state of the enterprise. This is achieved by performing a gap analysis. As noted in Chapter 1, the IT organization should have identified this at a high level, but it may be necessary to further define these objectives at a more concrete and practical level. This may require a substantial amount of effort, but it is a critical component in developing the security program.

texts.orig: If a program is established and has been functioning well, it is likely that many security program functions will already be accepted practice. Nevertheless, it will be useful to determine whether responsibilities are clearly defined and well documented. In many instances, a prior manager will have assumed a variety of functions and taken on responsibilities that were not formally defined and documented. Such managers may have been effective through being persuasive and influential rather than through defined and documented processes and structures. If the prior manager is available for orientation, it would be prudent to use whatever time is available to gain insight into the existing situation. If the prior manager is not available, it may take a thorough investigation to determine what the manager's responsibilities were and how tasks were accomplished.

texts.orig: Information security is a joint responsibility of business, information security and IT management and is integrated with corporate business objectives. Information security requirements are clearly defined, optimized and included in a verified security plan. Security functions are integrated with applications at the design stage and end users are increasingly accountable for managing security. Information security reporting provides early warning of changing and emerging risk, using automated active monitoring approaches for critical systems. Incidents are promptly addressed with formalized incident response procedures supported by automated tools. Periodic security assessments evaluate the effectiveness of implementation of the security plan. Information on new threats and vulnerabilities is systematically collected and analyzed, and adequate mitigating controls are promptly communicated and implemented. Intrusion testing, root cause analysis of security incidents and proactive identification of risk are the basis for continuous improvements. Security processes and technologies are integrated enterprise-wide.

texts.orig: Historically, some enterprise leaders have failed to recognize information security risk as requiring the same level of governance and oversight as other critical risks, and instead have viewed IT risk as a low-level, technology-based cost center. While universally recognized as necessary, information security has been viewed as an impediment to getting the job done. In the past, this viewpoint was accentuated by information security personnel who failed to achieve balance between risk treatment and efficient operations. Thankfully, this trend is diminishing, yet in many enterprises this historic misunderstanding may have produced a challenging environment for an information security manager. A few common manifestations of such an environment include lack of management support, poor resource levels for information security, a shortsighted approach to strategy and poor cooperation from other business units. Typically, the information security manager in this situation reports far down in the hierarchy and has the daunting task of trying to drive security up the organizational structure.

Typically, the information security manager in this situation reports far down in the hierarchy and has the daunting task of trying to drive security up the organizational structure.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The situation is gradually changing for the better for a number of reasons, including legal and regulatory mandates that require improved security as a matter of national security and commercial necessity. Expectations of customers and business partners are an important consideration that has provided a positive push toward enhanced security. Another is the credit card industry's rigorous security requirements from the PCI DSS council for enterprises that process credit card information. Since these requirements impact a very wide range of enterprises, they are likely to significantly improve many aspects of information security globally. Matching the rate of adoption and improved security to the pace of increasingly sophisticated and profitable criminal elements remains a challenge.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Although the overall situation in terms of security is improving, the information security manager must deal with the situation as it exists. Regardless of organizational circumstances, a persuasive information security manager with a clear vision of the role of information security in the enterprise can often improve the overall security posture with an ongoing campaign to educate stakeholders in the role and relevance of information security. This includes defining and seeking agreement on information risk control objectives, determining the enterprise's risk appetite and identifying mission-critical information assets.

texts.orig: It is beneficial for information security activities to align with and support defined business objectives. This is most effective if it is an ongoing effort and suitably communicated to stakeholders. Developing meaningful KPIs and metrics is also useful in supporting information security objectives. Each information security manager must determine the appropriate breadth and depth of metrics for the enterprise to provide the information needed for management. Information security managers should also implement some form of consistent reporting to promote awareness of the importance of information security management for the achievement of organizational objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Other issues the information security manager may need to deal with occur in situations in which the role of information security has been elevated within an enterprise. Even for mature information security programs, requirements and demands are rapidly changing, driven by technical and regulatory pressures. The challenges described in the following sections do not represent an exhaustive list, but they do illustrate methods for assessing and addressing several of the most common concerns. The information security manager should be cognizant of common challenges to effective information security management, the reasons behind those challenges and the strategies for addressing them.

texts.orig: Management Support
texts.text: Management Support

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Lack of management support is most common in smaller enterprises or in those of any size that are not in securityintensive industries. Such enterprises often have no compulsory requirement to address information security and, therefore, often view it as a marginally important issue that adds cost with little value. Those views often reflect a misunderstanding of the enterprise's dependence on information systems, the threat and risk environment, or the impact the enterprise may face or could already be unknowingly experiencing.
texts.text: Lack of management support is most common in smaller enterprises or in those of any size that are not in securityintensive industries. Such enterprises often have no compulsory requirement to address information security and, therefore, often view it as a marginally important issue that adds cost with little value. Those views often reflect a misunderstanding of the enterprise's dependence on information systems, the threat and risk environment, or the impact the enterprise may face or could already be unknowingly experiencing.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In such circumstances, the information security manager must use resources such as industry statistics, organizational impact and dependency analyses and reviews of common threats to the enterprise's specific information processing systems. In addition, management may require guidance on what actions are expected and information on approaches industry peers are taking to address information security. Even if initial education does not result in immediate strengthening of support, ongoing education should still be conducted to develop awareness of security needs.

Management support requires an ongoing dialogue with periodic review of objectives and strategy. Without regular updates, changes to business priorities may reduce the actual or perceived alignment of security priorities with those business needs and objectives.

While this issue may be a symptom of an underlying lack of management support, there are often other factors the information security manager is able to influence. Some funding-related issues that may need to be addressed by the information security manager include:
texts.text: Inadequate funding for information security initiatives is one of the most frustrating and challenging issues the information security manager must address. It is essential for the information security manager to find ways to show that security is important, functional and business-related.

texts.orig: 3.2.5 Common Information Security Program Constraints
texts.text: 3.2.5 Common Information Security Program Constraints

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In addition to the challenges mentioned, there are numerous overarching constraints that should be considered while developing an information security program. They will set the boundaries for the options available and should be thoroughly understood before initiating program development.
texts.text: In addition to the challenges mentioned, there are numerous overarching constraints that should be considered while developing an information security program. texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Physical
texts.text: Physical

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A variety of physical and environmental factors may influence or constrain an information security program. The obvious ones include capacity, space, environmental hazards and availability of infrastructure. The security strategy and program should make certain that provisions are made for the consideration of environmental hazards and adequate infrastructure capacity. texts.orig: 3.3.3 Information Asset Classification
texts.text: 3.3.3 Information Asset Classification

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information asset classification is required to determine the relative sensitivity and criticality of information assets, sometimes referred to collectively as business value. Criticality is determined by the impact on the enterprise as a result of the loss of an asset (i.e., how important the asset is to the business). Sensitivity is based on the potential damage to the enterprise as a result of unauthorized disclosure. It provides the basis for protection efforts, business continuity planning and user access control. For larger enterprises, information asset classification can be a daunting task because there are likely to be vast amounts of electronic data, warehouses of documents and thousands of individuals and devices. Yet, without determining the business value, sensitivity and criticality of information resources (and, increasingly, their related legal and regulatory requirements), it is not possible to develop an effective risk management program that provides appropriate protection proportional to business value or sensitivity and criticality.

Because this is also a necessary step in the risk identification phase of a risk assessment, it is an essential activity. In many enterprises, it may prove difficult to carry out, because there is often no comprehensive inventory of information-related assets. This is especially true in larger enterprises with multiple independent business units lacking a strong centralized security function. The identification process must determine the location of the data, the data owners, data users and data custodians. The security manager must also determine what data are housed by external service providers including cloud-hosted environments and Software as a Service applications like payroll services or health insurance administration. Service providers may also include media vaulting and archival firms, mailing list processors, firms that process mail containing company information, firms that act as couriers or transporters of information, and third-party service providers.

Because this is also a necessary step in the risk identification phase of a risk assessment, it is an essential activity. In many enterprises, it may prove difficult to carry out, because there is often no comprehensive inventory of information-related assets. This is especially true in larger enterprises with multiple independent business units lacking a strong centralized security function. The identification process must determine the location of the data, the data owners, data users and data custodians. The security manager must also determine what data are housed by external service providers including cloud-hosted environments and Software as a Service applications like payroll services or health insurance administration. Service providers may also include media vaulting and archival firms, mailing list processors, firms that process mail containing company information, firms that act as couriers or transporters of information, and third-party service providers.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Coordination with business unit managers should include determination of the appropriate information classification based on business value or levels of sensitivity and criticality of information assets. It should ensure that all business and IT stakeholders have the opportunity to review and approve the established guidelines for access control levels. The number of levels should be kept to a minimum, and classifications should be simple—e.g., designations by differing degrees for sensitivity and criticality. End-user managers, in coordination with the security administrator, can use these classifications in their risk and impact assessment process and to determine access levels of users. The information security manager must be aware that in a risk-averse enterprise or one with a blame culture there will be an incentive to overclassify, and it will be necessary to consider controls to limit this tendency.

texts.orig: A major benefit of information asset classification is the fact that tying security to business objectives reduces the risk of either underprotection or costly overprotection of information assets. The long-term benefits to the enterprise are substantial; the alternative is to provide all information assets with the same level of protection, which is unlikely to be cost-effective. If the enterprise is risk-averse and requires a high level of security, providing the same high level of protection to all assets can be very costly.

texts.orig: A number of methods exist to determine the sensitivity and criticality of information resources and the impact of adverse events. Methods outlined within COBIT, NIST and other frameworks are representative of the resources the information security manager may use.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is a generally accepted practice to focus on the impact that a loss of information assets has on the enterprise rather than on a specific adverse event. Because numerous adverse events could occur, it is not practical or cost-effective to list them all. It is important, however, to ensure that considerations include both the direct impact (such as a service outage or information disclosure) and any downstream consequences (like regulatory penalties or loss of customer confidence).

texts.orig: 3.4.1 Enterprise Information Security Architectures
texts.text: 3.4.1 Enterprise Information Security Architectures

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An enterprise information security architecture (EISA) can be a powerful tool for the development, implementation and integration of a strategy. The effectiveness of an EISA depends on it being an integral part of enterprise architecture (EA). It helps ensure that proper controls are implemented and integrated throughout the enterprise's infrastructure, processes and technologies.
texts.text: An enterprise information security architecture (EISA) can be a powerful tool for the development, implementation and integration of a strategy. The effectiveness of an EISA depends on it being an integral part of enterprise architecture (EA). It helps ensure that proper controls are implemented and integrated throughout the enterprise's infrastructure, processes and technologies.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The failure of enterprises to embrace the notion of security architecture appears to have several identifiable causes. One is that such projects are expensive and timeconsuming, and there is little or no understanding or appreciation at most organizational levels for the necessity or the potential benefits.
texts.text: The failure of enterprises to embrace the notion of security architecture appears to have several identifiable causes. One is that such projects are expensive and timeconsuming, and there is little or no understanding or appreciation at most organizational levels for the necessity or the potential benefits.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It may also be that there are few competent security architects with sufficiently broad and deep experience to address the wide range of issues necessary to ensure a reasonable degree of success. This lack of architecture over time has resulted in functionally less security integration and increasing vulnerability across the enterprise even though technical security has significantly improved. This lack of integration contributes to the increasing difficulty in managing enterprise security efforts effectively. Given the complexity of implementing an information security architecture as a framework to manage the complexity, it is recommended that the information security manager obtain assistance from enterprise architects. Guidance from those with expertise and understanding of architecture development will help ensure that the complex integration with information and technology will remain relevant and pragmatic as conditions evolve.

texts.orig: Several architectural approaches have been developed for the enterprise, all of which include essential aspects of security and some of which deal exclusively with security. While a detailed discussion of each of these approaches is beyond the scope of this manual, it should be noted that these approaches fall into three basic categories: process approaches, frameworks and reference models. Frameworks such as COBIT, the Zachman framework, Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture (SABSA) and The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) allow a great deal of flexibility in how each element of the architecture is developed. The essence of the frameworks is to describe the elements of architecture and how they must relate to each other. Process models are more directive in the processes used for the various elements. Reference models are a small-scale representation of the actual implementation. While the objectives of all the models are essentially the same, their approaches vary widely.

texts.orig: TOGAF addresses the following four interrelated areas of specialization, called architecture domains:
texts.text: TOGAF addresses the following four interrelated areas of specialization, called architecture domains:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Business architecture, which defines the business strategy, governance, organization and key business processes of the enterprise
texts.text: Business architecture, which defines the business strategy, governance, organization and key business processes of the enterprise

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Applications architecture, which provides a blueprint for the individual application systems to be deployed, the interactions among the application systems, and their relationships to the core business processes of the enterprise with the frameworks for services to be exposed as business functions for integration
texts.text: Applications architecture, which provides a blueprint for the individual application systems to be deployed, the interactions among the application systems, and their relationships to the core business processes of the enterprise with the frameworks for services to be exposed as business functions for integration

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Data architecture, which describes the structure of an enterprise's logical and physical data assets and the associated data management resources
texts.text: Data architecture, which describes the structure of an enterprise's logical and physical data assets and the associated data management resources

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Technical architecture, or technology architecture, which describes the hardware, software and network infrastructure needed to support the deployment of core mission-critical applications
texts.text: Technical architecture, or technology architecture, which describes the hardware, software and network infrastructure needed to support the deployment of core mission-critical applications

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The objectives of the various approaches are essentially the same. The framework details the organization, roles, entities and relationships that exist, or should exist, to perform a set of business processes. The framework should provide a rigorous taxonomy that clearly identifies what processes a business performs and includes detailed information about how those processes are executed and secured. The end product is a set of artifacts that describe, in varying degrees of detail, exactly what and how a business operates and what security controls are required.

The framework details the organization, roles, entities and relationships that exist, or should exist, to perform a set of business processes. The framework should provide a rigorous taxonomy that clearly identifies what processes a business performs and includes detailed information about how those processes are executed and secured. The end product is a set of artifacts that describe, in varying degrees of detail, exactly what and how a business operates and what security controls are required.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The choice of approaches may be limited by an existing organizational standard, but if one does not exist, the choice should be made based on form, fit and function. In other words, a particular approach may be more consistent with existing organizational practices or may be more suitable for a particular situation. The various approaches may also entail considerably greater efforts and resources. Some are more oriented to or limited to technical architectures and will not be well suited for governance purposes.

texts.orig: While a specific security architecture may be of considerable benefit, it is essential that it be guided by, and tightly integrated with, the overall enterprise architecture. A current enterprise architecture, such as TOGAF (figure 3.9), will address security as an essential component of the overall design and, in most cases, will be the preferred approach to ensure effective integration.

texts.orig: The TOGAF Architecture Development Method (ADM) phases, as shown in figure 3.10, include:
texts.text: The TOGAF Architecture Development Method (ADM) phases, as shown in figure 3.10, include:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Preliminary phase—Deals mainly with the definition of the architecture framework and the architecture principles. In addition, the overall scope, constraints, objectives and assumptions are identified.
texts.text: Preliminary phase—Deals mainly with the definition of the architecture framework and the architecture principles. In addition, the overall scope, constraints, objectives and assumptions are identified.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Architecture vision—Deals with defining the vision and scope of the architecture and specific segments of work to be performed.
texts.text: Architecture vision—Deals with defining the vision and scope of the architecture and specific segments of work to be performed.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Business architecture—Addresses the description of the as-is business architecture domain, the development of the to-be business architecture and the gap analysis between the two.
texts.text: Business architecture—Addresses the description of the as-is business architecture domain, the development of the to-be business architecture and the gap analysis between the two.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Information systems architecture—Provides the description of the as-is and to-be data, applications domains and conducting the gap analyses.
texts.text: Information systems architecture—Provides the description of the as-is and to-be data, applications domains and conducting the gap analyses.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Technology architecture—Deals with the description of the as-is and to-be technology domains and conducting a gap analysis.
texts.text: Technology architecture—Deals with the description of the as-is and to-be technology domains and conducting a gap analysis.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Opportunities and solutions—Deals with the formulation of a high-level implementation and migration strategy to transform the as-is architecture into the to-be architecture.
texts.text: Opportunities and solutions—Deals with the formulation of a high-level implementation and migration strategy to transform the as-is architecture into the to-be architecture.

texts.label: list_item

texts.orig: There are four commonly accepted subsets of an overall enterprise architecture:
texts.text: There are four commonly accepted subsets of an overall enterprise architecture:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ● A business (or business process) architecture defines the business strategy, governance, organization and key business processes.
texts.text: A business (or business process) architecture defines the business strategy, governance, organization and key business processes.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ● A data architecture describes the structure of an enterprise's logical and physical data assets and data management resources.
texts.text: A data architecture describes the structure of an enterprise's logical and physical data assets and data management resources.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: An applications architecture provides a blueprint for the individual application systems to be deployed, their interactions, and their relationships to the core business processes of the enterprise.
texts.text: An applications architecture provides a blueprint for the individual application systems to be deployed, their interactions, and their relationships to the core business processes of the enterprise.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: A technology architecture describes the architectural ● principles, component relationships, and hardware and software infrastructure intended to support the deployment of core, mission-critical applications.
texts.text: A technology architecture describes the architectural ● principles, component relationships, and hardware and software infrastructure intended to support the deployment of core, mission-critical applications.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Whatever architectural approach is chosen, an effective approach must start with the enterprise business architecture. The subsequent designs—such as application, security and data architectures—function as subsets to ensure alignment with and support of business strategy and objectives.
texts.text: Whatever architectural approach is chosen, an effective approach must start with the enterprise business architecture. The subsequent designs—such as application, security and data architectures—function as subsets to ensure alignment with and support of business strategy and objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The complexity of developing and implementing some approaches has proven to be a hindrance to adoption. For example, some notions of information security architecture frameworks include six layers, from contextual to physical. Like a building architecture, the highest or contextual level defined in SABSA and the Zachman frameworks is the "business" or utility layer (i.e., what the structure is to be used for). A theater is designed very differently from an office building because the buildings are used for different purposes. The design, or architecture, is tightly aligned with the purpose (i.e., linked to the business objective). The contextual architecture serves to define the relationships among various required business attributes. These include who, what, when, where and how, which drive the next layer—the conceptual layer—which integrates the architectural design concepts with the business requirements.

texts.orig: The important consideration, regardless of the approach, is that at the point of the development and implementation of an information security program, some form of high-level architecture or design should be in place. This is particularly the case for major implementations comprised of many parts and projects that must integrate well to achieve program objectives. Although many enterprises do not have them, the adoption of an appropriate enterprise or security architecture can be essential to developing and implementing an effective information security program.

texts.orig: 3.4.2 Information Security Management Frameworks
texts.text: 3.4.2 Information Security Management Frameworks

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The information security management framework is a conceptual representation of an information security management structure. It should define the technical, operational, managerial, administrative and educational components of the program; the organizational units and leadership responsible for each component; the control or management objective that each component should deliver; the interfaces and information flow among the components; and each component's tangible outputs. Although formats and detail levels vary, the framework should fundamentally describe the information security management components (e.g., roles, policies, standard operating procedures [SOPs], management procedures, security architectures) and their interactions in broad strokes: This is, in essence, an operational architecture as described in Section 3.4.1 Enterprise Information Security Architectures.
texts.text: The information security management framework is a conceptual representation of an information security management structure. It should define the technical, operational, managerial, administrative and educational components of the program; the organizational units and leadership responsible for each component; the control or management objective that each component should deliver; the interfaces and information flow among the components; and each component's tangible outputs. Although formats and detail levels vary, the framework should fundamentally describe the information security management components (e.g., roles, policies, standard operating procedures [SOPs], management procedures, security architectures) and their interactions in broad strokes: This is, in essence, an operational architecture as described in Section 3.4.1 Enterprise Information Security Architectures.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Other outcomes of an effective security management framework focus on shorter-term needs. For example, organizational decision makers require awareness of risk and mitigation options in support of corporate initiatives such as external hosting of information systems. Implementers of solutions often require the services of technical security subject matter experts, which the information security manager should facilitate either through internal or external resources. Ensuring that initiatives and existing operations adhere to policies and standards is also a responsibility that the information security manager and the security department are expected to manage.

texts.orig: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
texts.text: NIST Cybersecurity Framework

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Formally titled the NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, this model provides high-level guidance for aligning a cybersecurity program with enterprise objectives. In response to an increasing prevalence of cybersecurity attacks, NIST convened a series of workshops to develop a process by which an enterprise could identify opportunities for improvement in the information security program. The framework highlights the need for effective risk management integration and it broadly supports improvement in supply chain risk management.
texts.text: Formally titled the NIST Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity, this model provides high-level guidance for aligning a cybersecurity program with enterprise objectives. In response to an increasing prevalence of cybersecurity attacks, NIST convened a series of workshops to develop a process by which an enterprise could identify opportunities for improvement in the information security program. The framework highlights the need for effective risk management integration and it broadly supports improvement in supply chain risk management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework does not provide controls to be applied. Instead, it guides practitioners through the process of determining gaps between the current state of practice and a desired target state that might better fulfill enterprise mission, including risk management needs. Analysis of the gaps between states enables the use of controls-based frameworks (including those listed herein) to improve information security risk management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Components of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework include:
texts.text: Components of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework include:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ● The Framework Core—a set of cybersecurity-related outcomes organized in terms of five concurrent functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. When considered together, these functions provide a high-level, strategic view of the life cycle of an enterprise's management of cybersecurity risk. The Framework Core then identifies underlying key categories and subcategories for each function. To provide clarity regarding the intended outcomes of each subcategory, NIST provides examples (or informative references) from well-known standards, guidelines and practices, including several mentioned previously.

The tiers characterize an enterprise's practices over a range from Partial (Tier 1) to Adaptive (Tier 4). These tiers reflect a progression from informal, reactive responses to approaches that are agile and risk-informed. Coordination with enterprise stakeholders to select a desired tier

texts.orig: NIST Risk Management Framework
texts.text: NIST Risk Management Framework

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF) provides a process that integrates security, privacy, and cyber supply chain risk management activities into the system development life cycle. Originally intended to help US government agencies to evaluate and improve information security, it has been broadened to apply to any enterprise and is available without cost. The RMF provides a risk-based approach to the categorization of relevant assets, selection and implementation of controls to achieve adequate protection, and provisions for monitoring the continued effectiveness and efficiency of risk management measures.

Originally intended to help US government agencies to evaluate and improve information security, it has been broadened to apply to any enterprise and is available without cost. The RMF provides a risk-based approach to the categorization of relevant assets, selection and implementation of controls to achieve adequate protection, and provisions for monitoring the continued effectiveness and efficiency of risk management measures.

texts.orig: The RMF consists of seven steps:
texts.text: The RMF consists of seven steps:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Prepare for applying the framework by determining enterprise goals and objectives, relevant risk management roles, enterprise risk strategy and policy directives, organizational artifacts regarding risk assessment (existing and planned) and methods for monitoring and communicating risk activities and results.
texts.text: Prepare for applying the framework by determining enterprise goals and objectives, relevant risk management roles, enterprise risk strategy and policy directives, organizational artifacts regarding risk assessment (existing and planned) and methods for monitoring and communicating risk activities and results.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ● Categorize the system and information processed, stored and transmitted based on an analysis of the impact of the loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability of that system or information.
texts.text: Categorize the system and information processed, stored and transmitted based on an analysis of the impact of the loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability of that system or information.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ● Select the set of security and privacy controls (generally published in NIST Special Publication 800-53) that will achieve the appropriate risk management objectives in light of the categorization. Baseline sets of controls are provided in a separate document as a starting point, and they can then be tailored to achieve risk management objectives. Similar processes are available for shared controls that may be used by various entities throughout the enterprise.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 3.4.3 Information Security Framework Components
texts.text: 3.4.3 Information Security Framework Components

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Most standard frameworks for information security show the development of an information security program as starting with risk assessment and the identification of control objectives and key controls defined by standards such as COBIT and ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002. While guidance is provided by these standards, control objectives must be based on individual organizational objectives and risk appetite and tolerance tailored to achieve the desired outcomes. As the program develops and matures and conditions change, control objectives may need to be changed and additional or modified controls may be required to address new conditions, emerging risk, evolving regulations or contractual obligations.

While guidance is provided by these standards, control objectives must be based on individual organizational objectives and risk appetite and tolerance tailored to achieve the desired outcomes. As the program develops and matures and conditions change, control objectives may need to be changed and additional or modified controls may be required to address new conditions, emerging risk, evolving regulations or contractual obligations.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The various components that make up the management framework can be broken down into their functional elements (i.e., technical, operational, managerial, administrative and educational components). This can be helpful in ensuring that each aspect is adequately represented in the framework and given appropriate security consideration.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Technical Components
texts.text: Technical Components

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security is typically involved in most or all of the technical IT components of an enterprise, including providing and maintaining suitable security standards, reviewing procedures for policy compliance, designing and implementing appropriate security metrics, and providing general oversight. Many of the key controls identified in the framework address risk associated with the technical components, including their configuration, monitoring, maintenance and operation. While IT may own the systems, IT is typically not the data owner and serves as custodian with a requirement to provide adequate protection and compliance with the enterprise's information security policies by operating within the applicable standards. In other cases, the business owner may actually own the systems supporting the business operation but, in either case, IT will still serve as custodian. It is essential that all technology components have an identified owner and that there are no orphan systems. This is necessary to ensure responsibility and accountability for maintaining all systems in compliance with security policies and for ownership and proper treatment of associated risk to acceptable levels.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Operational components of a security program are the ongoing management and administrative activities that must be performed to provide the required level of security assurance. These operational components include items such as SOPs, business operation security practices, and maintenance and administration of security technologies. They are generally conducted on a daily to weekly timeline.

texts.label: text

Because it is common for many of these components to fall outside the direct control of the information security department (e.g., operating system patching procedures), the information security manager must work with and provide oversight for IT, business units and other organizational groups to ensure that operational security needs are covered. texts.label: text

These typically include strategic implementation activities such as standards development or modification, policy reviews, and oversight of initiatives or program execution. These are activities that generally take place less frequently than operational components, perhaps on a timeline measured in months, quarters or years.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Management objectives, requirements and policies are key in shaping the rest of the information security program, which, in turn, defines what must be managed. The information security manager must ensure that the program development process is executed with appropriate consideration to legal, regulatory, risk and resource issues, and a suite of metrics necessary for decision support.

The information security manager must ensure that the program development process is executed with appropriate consideration to legal, regulatory, risk and resource issues, and a suite of metrics necessary for decision support.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ongoing or periodic analysis of assets, threats, risk and organizational impacts must continue to be the basis for modifying security policies and developing or modifying standards. texts.label: text
texts.orig: As the scope and responsibilities of the information security management function grow, so do the resources, personnel and financial aspects involved. This means that information security management must address the same business administration activities as other business units. The information security manager in charge of such an operation must ensure that financial, HR and other management functions are effective.

This means that information security management must address the same business administration activities as other business units. The information security manager in charge of such an operation must ensure that financial, HR and other management functions are effective.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Financial administration functions generally consist of budgeting, timeline planning, TCO analysis/management, ROI analysis/management, acquisition/purchasing and inventory management. These functions, particularly budgeting and timeline planning, often require updates throughout the fiscal year as financial realities and organizational goals change. The information security manager should establish a working rapport with the enterprise's finance department to ensure a strong working relationship, support, and compliance with financial policies and procedures.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: HR management functions generally include job description management, organizational planning, recruitment and hiring, performance management, payroll and time tracking administration, employee education and development, and termination management. The information security program should account for the time and resources needed for these activities, particularly as program staffing grows over time. Those charged with management of larger information security programs must also address the need to develop an efficient organizational structure with appropriate layers of management and supervisory personnel. In all issues related to HR management, it is important for the information security manager to work closely with HR leadership and adhere to established procedures to prevent legal liabilities and other types of risk.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Effective management functions require the information security manager to balance project efforts and ongoing operational overhead with staff head count, utilization levels and external resources. Rarely does any information security program have an optimal number of resources, and it is always necessary to prioritize efforts. The information security manager should work with the steering committee and executive management to determine priorities and establish consensus on what project items may be delayed because of resource constraints. Spikes in activity or unexpected project efforts can often be addressed with third-party resources such as contractors. The information security manager should maintain relationships with the vendors most likely to be engaged in such cases.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is not unusual for the information security manager to be under pressure to shortcut security management, quality assurance (QA) and development processes or to divert resources from daily operations to accelerate project efforts. It is the role of the information security manager to document and ensure that executive management understands the risk implications of moving an initiative ahead without full security diligence; it is up to executive management to decide if the initiative is important enough to warrant the risk. If this situation occurs, the information security manager should make every effort to utilize the first available opportunity to revisit systems or initiatives that are not certified or accredited.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Employee education and awareness regarding security risk is often integrated with employee orientation and initial training. General organizational policies and procedures, such as acceptable use policies and employee monitoring policies, should be communicated and administered at the enterprise's HR level. Issues and responsibilities that are specific to an employee's role or enterprise (e.g., call center authentication of customers) should be communicated and administered at the business unit level. Interactive education techniques, such as online testing and role-playing, are often more effective than a purely informational approach. Examples of these types of training include incident response and contingency plan training and exercises. In all cases, the information security manager should collaborate with HR and business units to identify information security education needs. Pertinent metrics (e.g., average employee quiz scores, average time elapsed since last employee training) should be tracked and communicated to the steering committee and executive management.

texts.orig: One of the most important aspects of the action plan to execute the strategy is to create or modify policies and standards as needed. Policies must capture the intent, expectations and direction of management. As a strategy evolves, it is vital that supporting policies are developed to articulate the strategy. For example, if the objective is to become ISO/IEC 27001:2013-compliant over a threeyear period, then the strategy must consider which elements are addressed first, which resources are allocated, how the elements of the standard can be accomplished and so forth. The road map should show the steps and the sequence, dependencies and milestones. The action plan is essentially a project plan to implement the strategy following the road map.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When considering security control objectives, a systems architect can use combinations of technologies to provide control points in a system's infrastructure. Combined with control activities and associated procedures, these control points may be used to ensure that policy compliance is preserved as new systems that use the infrastructure are deployed. For example, if a network is structured so there is only one connection to the Internet, then all network traffic destined for the Internet must travel through that connection. This would allow technology to be deployed in one place where all documents destined for the Internet could be inspected to ensure authorization to send the information contained in the document to an external entity. Often, no technology will be specified by the architecture, leaving a wide range of design choices for control points for inspection of documents being sent to the Internet.

texts.orig: There are multiple alternatives that an application may employ to achieve the level of client identification necessary to mitigate the risk of impersonation. In financial applications such as online banking, regulators require that banks use some form of multifactor authentication to provide additional assurance of the identity of the individual initiating the client request. Applying this requirement uniformly on all applications (making it part of the enterprise's security architecture) allows the enterprise to mitigate the impersonation threat in a uniform, efficient and supportable manner. A number of approaches to architecture for components of information systems exist (e.g., architectures for data and databases, servers, technical infrastructures, identity management). However, few enterprises have developed an overall comprehensive enterprise security architecture, structured its management, and defined its relationship to business objectives. This is somewhat analogous to a situation in which separate, unintegrated designs for aircraft wings, engines, navigational equipment, passenger seats, etc., exist, but there are no designs for the complete aircraft showing how the various components fit together. The result would be unlikely to function well, if at all, and the outcome would be untrustworthy. Admittedly, information systems are designed to operate in a far more loosely coupled fashion, but the point is, nevertheless, relevant.

texts.orig: In the typical enterprise, information security program management includes short- and long-range planning and day-to-day administration in addition to directing various projects and initiatives. It also includes a variety of risk management activities and incident management and response functions and a variety of oversight and monitoring functions. Program management typically includes aspects of governance—whether in terms of policy and standards development or procedural controls and general rules of use for end users. As with other aspects of information security, governance cannot remain static in a changing risk environment and must evolve to be effective.
