texts.label: text
texts.orig: The fundamental purpose of contracts is twofold: 1) to ensure that the parties to the agreement are aware of their responsibilities and rights within the relationship; and 2) to provide the means to address disagreements once the contract is in force. Within that framework, the information security manager should be familiar with certain provisions for security and information protection. While the information security manager may or may not be included in contract reviews, the following issues should be addressed with the legal department to ensure an understanding of security requirements that should be covered.
texts.text: The fundamental purpose of contracts is twofold: 1) to ensure that the parties to the agreement are aware of their responsibilities and rights within the relationship; and 2) to provide the means to address disagreements once the contract is in force. Within that framework, the information security manager should be familiar with certain provisions for security and information protection. While the information security manager may or may not be included in contract reviews, the following issues should be addressed with the legal department to ensure an understanding of security requirements that should be covered.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The most common security provision addresses confidentiality or nondisclosure. Each party will typically agree that any confidential or sensitive information it receives as part of the agreement, or about the other party, will be kept confidential through appropriate measures. This may also include the requirement to return or destroy any proprietary or confidential information upon termination of the contract or after a specified period of time. The information security manager will need to determine the specific level of destruction that will be required (e.g., document shredding, disk and tape degaussing).

Each party will typically agree that any confidential or sensitive information it receives as part of the agreement, or about the other party, will be kept confidential through appropriate measures. The information security manager will need to determine the specific level of destruction that will be required (e.g., document shredding, disk and tape degaussing).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The contract may also stipulate that either or both parties must maintain security controls to ensure that the systems and information used under the agreement are protected by appropriate means. The contract should exp t t   s   the requirements for demonstrating the effectiveness of those protections. Whether it is through the production of a current third-party audit report (e.g., SSAE16) or compliance with an industry-standard security framework (such as ISO/IEC 2700X or COBIT), the standards by which the program will be judged should be defined in the contract. Additionally, if the contracted product or service includes network connectivity between the buyer and the seller, the contract should address responsibility for the security of that connection. Specifications as to the level of security expected (e.g., firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention, monitoring) or specific technical requirements should also be addressed.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A contract with a service provider that has been determined (through a risk assessment) to be beyond a predetermined risk threshold should always contain provisions concerning right-to-audit and a right-toinspect without notice. This would typically be for any third party that accesses, stores or processes any sensitive or otherwise business-critical information; provides mission-critical services; or connects to the network infrastructure of the contracting enterprise. The right-to-audit clause should allow the customer, upon proper notice, the right to conduct an in-depth audit of the third party's security program and processes to verify the effectiveness of all associated controls. The right-toinspect without notice, although not generally favored by service providers, can provide greater incentive to adhere to contractual requirements on an ongoing basis. If these provisions are included in the contract, the parameters for an audit, such as compliance criteria, notification, scope limitations, frequency and responsibility for incurred costs, should be explicit. The right to inspect should ideally have few, if any, constraints.

texts.orig: In the event that a security breach happens at either party, the contract should specify the roles each party will play in the investigation and remediation process. Issues such as which party will lead the investigation, notification procedures and responsibilities (including law enforcement or regulatory notifications), and timing must all be addressed. During an active incident, pressure is high, tempers can flare and fairness and equity are much harder to come by, so addressing these issues in the contract is easier and can be done much more equitably.

texts.orig: Finally, the contract should contain indemnity clauses that ensure compensation for impacts caused by the service provider. Service providers will typically attempt to limit compensation for their failure to specific amounts or, in some cases, to the amount of fees paid to them for a specific period, such as the past 12 months. Such limits are not in the best interests of the contracting enterprise. Another consideration is what are called choice of law provisions, which require that any potential litigation take place in certain jurisdictions, typically favorable to the service provider. While these elements are in the purview of the legal department (if there is one, which may not be the case in a small enterprise), it is useful for the information security manager to have an understanding of these issues.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Third-party access to the processing facilities of the information security manager's enterprise under any circumstances should be controlled based on risk assessment and must be clearly defined in an SLA. Access should be granted based on the principles of least privilege, need-to-know and need-to-do. It is important to bear in mind that third parties may have a different business culture and set of ethics, which must be considered in terms of risk.

texts.text: 3.14 Information Security Program Communications and Reporting

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Among the most important outcomes of the information security program are effective communications and reporting regarding the successful achievement of security and privacy objectives, ongoing risk status, and opportunities for improvement. Senior leaders have a responsibility to remain aware of various risk factors. For some, failure to stay current could result in prison or financial penalties. Through various assessment, monitoring and reporting techniques, the information security manager can fulfill the commitments made in the business case, demonstrate successful implementation of the security strategy, and ensure that relevant stakeholders are always informed regarding results of ongoing monitoring.

texts.orig: 3.14.2 The Plan-Do-Check-Act Cycle
texts.text: 3.14.2 The Plan-Do-Check-Act Cycle

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The information security program is based on the effective, efficient management of controls designed and implemented to treat or mitigate threats, risk, vulnerabilities and impacts. The unique dependency on the effective, efficient management of a business process such as information security lends itself to the concepts and methodologies encompassed within the total quality management (TQM) system.
texts.text: The information security program is based on the effective, efficient management of controls designed and implemented to treat or mitigate threats, risk, vulnerabilities and impacts. The unique dependency on the effective, efficient management of a business process such as information security lends itself to the concepts and methodologies encompassed within the total quality management (TQM) system.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An important TQM outcome, originally developed by American physicist Walter Shewhart during the 1920s, was a four-step problem-solving iterative technique used to improve business processes. That cycle was adapted and popularized by quality control pioneer W. Edwards Deming in the 1950s. The cycle, which Deming called the Shewhart Cycle after his mentor, became the now famous tailored plan-do-check-act (PDCA) process. PDCA comprises four quality assessment and improvement processes, as depicted in figure 3.22.

texts.orig: Objective—A review objective is a statement of what is to be determined in the course of a review. For example, the objective of a review may be to determine whether an Internet banking application can be exploited to gain access to internal systems. Objectives define what the information security manager wants to get out of the review. Usually, it is to determine whether a given systems environment meets some security standard. In the preceding example, the review objective is that of a typical external penetration study (i.e., to make sure that users of web services cannot exploit system vulnerabilities to gain access to the systems that host those services).

texts.orig: Audits
texts.text: Audits

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Like security reviews, audits have objectives, scopes, constraints, approaches and results. The professional practice of information systems audit is based on an approach in which auditors identify, evaluate, test and assess the effectiveness of controls. Effectiveness is judged based on whether controls meet a given set of control objectives, such as compliance with policies and standards. In performing an audit, an audit team assembles documentation that: 1) maps controls to control objectives, 2) states what the team did to test those controls and 3) links those test results to the final assessment. This documentation, called work papers, may or may not be delivered with the final report.

texts.orig: When an information security program has established policies and standards, an audit is extremely useful in identifying whether those policies and standards have been fully implemented. However, when an information security program is under development, those policies and standards may not yet be finalized. In this situation, an information security manager may select an externally published standard and engage an audit team to determine the extent to which the enterprise is in compliance. An external standard or framework, such as COBIT or ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, provides a structure for control objectives that enables an audit team to organize its examination of existing controls. The work papers from such an audit can often be more useful than the final report. The value in the analysis of existing controls and their mapping to a set of external standards is most useful if the set of external standards closely resembles those the information security manager intends to put in place as part of the information security program.

texts.text: Auditors

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is essential for the information security manager to develop a good working relationship with the auditors, whether internal or external. While it is not unusual for auditors to be viewed in a negative light by IT and information security staff and others in the enterprise, effective information security managers understand that audits are both an essential assurance process and a critical and influential ally in achieving good security governance and compliance. They can be instrumental in implementing security standards by providing feedback to senior management through audit findings that can serve to influence the tone at the top and create highlevel support for security activities. Involving auditors in overall security management can be a powerful tool for improving an enterprise's security culture.

texts.orig: The information security program must integrate with internal and external auditing activities. Some audits are compulsory, such as those required to establish compliance with a regulatory standard. Others are voluntary, as when an independent auditor makes an attestation to compliance with an industry standard.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The information security manager should coordinate with organizational audit coordinators to ensure that time and resources are allocated to address audit activities. Procedures should be established in advance for scheduling, observation of employee activities, and provision of configuration data from technical systems.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In some cases, a deficiency identified by an auditor may not be applicable to the information security manager's specific enterprise. If concerns are identified during an audit, the information security manager should work with the auditors to agree on associated risk, mitigating factors and satisfactory control objectives. With this information in hand, the information security manager may craft one or more potential solutions that fit the enterprise's operational, financial and technical environment. Any combination of mitigating or compensating controls that enforce the agreed-on control objectives should satisfy the issue.

texts.text: 3.14.4 Compliance Monitoring and Enforcement

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Compliance enforcement processes must be considered during program development to ensure subsequent effectiveness and manageability once the program is implemented. Compliance enforcement refers to any activity within the information security program that is designed to ensure compliance with the enterprise's security policies, standards and procedures.
texts.text: Compliance enforcement processes must be considered during program development to ensure subsequent effectiveness and manageability once the program is implemented. Compliance enforcement refers to any activity within the information security program that is designed to ensure compliance with the enterprise's security policies, standards and procedures.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Compliance, especially with procedural controls, may pose one of the major challenges for managing a security program and must be given careful attention when designing controls during program development. Ease of monitoring and enforcement is often one of the essential factors in control selection. Complex control processes that are not readily enforceable or are difficult to monitor for compliance are generally of little value and may pose a considerable risk themselves.

texts.orig: Enforcement procedures should be designed to assume that control activities are in place in support of control objectives. These procedures provide an added layer of control to ensure that the procedures established by management are actually followed. For example, in a password reset procedure, an enforcement procedure may consist of a supervisor listening to randomly selected help desk calls and listing any help desk staff who neglected to ask a user for a security identification code prior to resetting a password. The enforcement procedure would be to use the list first to warn and then to discipline any help desk staff member who did not follow the password reset procedure.

texts.orig: Policy Compliance
texts.text: Policy Compliance

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Policies form the basis for all accountability with respect to security responsibilities throughout the enterprise. Policies must be comprehensive enough to cover all situations in which information is handled, yet flexible enough to allow different processes and procedures to evolve for different technologies and still be in compliance. Except in very small enterprises, an information security manager will not have direct control over SDLC activities of all information systems in the enterprise. Consequently, it is necessary to designate formal security roles that establish which department head is responsible for putting processes in place that maintain security policy compliance and meet the appropriate standards for a given set of information systems.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is the responsibility of the information security manager to ensure that, in the assignment process, there are no orphan systems or systems without policy compliance owners. It is also the responsibility of the information security manager to provide oversight and ensure that policy compliance processes are properly designed. An information security manager can accomplish this oversight via a combination of security review, metrics gathering and reporting processes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Information security management literature often refers to a policy exception process. This is a method by which business units or departments can review a policy and decide not to follow it based on various factors. Several justifications can exist for policy exceptions. An exception may be based on a risk/reward decision in which the benefit of not following the policy justifies the risk. It may be financially or technically infeasible to comply with specific policies or standards. Such tradeoffs should be considered in the policy development process, when possible, to minimize the need for subsequent exceptions. As part of the program development, a formal waiver process should be implemented to manage the life cycle of these exceptions to ensure they are periodically reviewed and, when possible, closed. Any such policy exceptions must be assessed for risk and impact prior to implementation and the identified risk accepted by appropriate levels of management.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Standards provide the boundaries of options for systems, processes and actions that still comply with policy. The standards must be designed to ensure that all systems of the same type within the same security domain are configured and operated in the same way based on criticality and sensitivity of the resources. These will allow platform administration procedures to be developed using standards documents as references to ensure that policy compliance is maintained. Standards also provide economy of scale; the configuration mapping to policy needs to be done only once for each security domain, and technology and process engineering efforts are reused for systems of the same type.

The standards must be designed to ensure that all systems of the same type within the same security domain are configured and operated in the same way based on criticality and sensitivity of the resources. These will allow platform administration procedures to be developed using standards documents as references to ensure that policy compliance is maintained. Standards also provide economy of scale; the configuration mapping to policy needs to be done only once for each security domain, and technology and process engineering efforts are reused for systems of the same type.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As much as possible, compliance with standards should be automated to ensure that system configurations do not, either intentionally or unintentionally, deviate from policy compliance. However, as policies should state only management intent, direction and expectations to allow flexibility for different standards to develop, and provide many options to comply, exceptions to standards should always be reviewed to see if they deviate from the intent of the policy. It may also be that a business situation justifies a deviation from existing standards but, nevertheless, may be determined to fall within the intent of the policy. As with policy exceptions, standards exceptions must include risk assessment and acceptance by appropriate management. If exceptions are required to go through the change management process (assuming one is in place), assessing the risk of the change will be a standard part of the process.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Compliance enforcement is an ongoing set of activities that endeavor to ensure policy and, by default, standards requirements that are not being met are brought into compliance. Audits are a snapshot of compliance in time; compliance enforcement is an ongoing process that helps reduce risk and ensure positive audit opinions.
texts.text: Compliance enforcement is an ongoing set of activities that endeavor to ensure policy and, by default, standards requirements that are not being met are brought into compliance. Audits are a snapshot of compliance in time; compliance enforcement is an ongoing process that helps reduce risk and ensure positive audit opinions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Compliance enforcement responsibilities are usually shared across organizational units and the results are commonly shared with executive management and the board's audit or compliance committees. The legal and internal audit departments often have responsibility for assessment of business strategies and operations, respectively. The information security unit is often responsible for implementing independent evaluation of technical standards, preferably using automated tools. In larger enterprises and heavily regulated industries, an independent compliance organization may be established to handle and coordinate these activities.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 3.14.5 Monitoring Approaches
texts.text: 3.14.5 Monitoring Approaches

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is important for the security manager to develop a consistent, reliable method to determine the overall ongoing effectiveness of the program. One way is to regularly conduct risk assessments and track improvements over time. Another standard tool is the use of external and internal scanning and penetration testing to determine system vulnerabilities, although this will indicate the effectiveness of only one facet of the overall program. Doing so on a regular basis and tracking the results can be a useful indicator of trends in technical security. Most enterprises conduct regular vulnerability scans to determine if open vulnerabilities are addressed and new ones appear. Steady improvement is the hallmark of an effective program, although it is of limited value from a management perspective unless it is accompanied by information about viable threats and potential impacts to provide enough information to inform appropriate security decisions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Because an enterprise's vulnerability to security breaches likely exists at all times, continuous monitoring of security activities is a prudent business practice (and increasingly a regulatory requirement) that the information security manager should implement. A great deal of this monitoring will be technical and may be performed by IT personnel. In this case, the monitoring requirements must be defined in suitable operating standards along with severity criteria and escalation processes.

In this case, the monitoring requirements must be defined in suitable operating standards along with severity criteria and escalation processes.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Measuring Compliance
texts.text: Measuring Compliance

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An essential, ongoing and primary concern for information security program management is policy and standards compliance. Given that most security failures are the result of personnel failing to follow procedures in compliance with standards, compliance is an essential element of security management. Criticality and sensitivity must be known, as they mandate the level of compliance that must be achieved to manage risk to acceptable levels. Anything less than 100 percent compliance is unacceptable when piloting passenger jets or operating nuclear power plants because impacts are likely to be catastrophic. For any activity that is not lifeor enterprise-threatening, the cost and level of compliance efforts must be weighed against the benefits and potential impacts.

Given that most security failures are the result of personnel failing to follow procedures in compliance with standards, compliance is an essential element of security management. Criticality and sensitivity must be known, as they mandate the level of compliance that must be achieved to manage risk to acceptable levels. Anything less than 100 percent compliance is unacceptable when piloting passenger jets or operating nuclear power plants because impacts are likely to be catastrophic. For any activity that is not lifeor enterprise-threatening, the cost and level of compliance efforts must be weighed against the benefits and potential impacts.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Measuring compliance with technical standards is often straightforward and can frequently be automated. Compliance with procedural or process standards is generally more difficult and may pose a challenge. Because this is frequently the area of failure leading to security compromise, it requires careful consideration. Some compliance requirements are sufficiently critical to warrant direct continuous monitoring, such as access controlled by guards and sign-in procedures. In other cases, detective controls such as logging and checklists may suffice.

Compliance with procedural or process standards is generally more difficult and may pose a challenge. Because this is frequently the area of failure leading to security compromise, it requires careful consideration. Some compliance requirements are sufficiently critical to warrant direct continuous monitoring, such as access controlled by guards and sign-in procedures. In other cases, detective controls such as logging and checklists may suffice.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Compliance requirements may be statutory, contractual or internal. If the enterprise must comply with compulsory or voluntary standards involving information security, the information security manager must ensure that program goals are aligned with those requirements. Likewise, the policies, procedures and technologies implemented by the program must fulfill requirements of adopted standards. Measurements of compliance achievement are often tied to the results of internal or external audits. The information security manager may wish to implement automated or manual compliance monitoring with higher frequency and/or broader scope than achievable with incremental audits. In addition to actual point-in-time compliance, the program should be measured on the effectiveness of resolving identified compliance issues.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Measuring Operational Productivity
texts.text: Measuring Operational Productivity

texts.label: text
texts.orig: No information security program has unlimited resources. It is crucial for the information security manger to maximize operational productivity, especially in light of the rapid growth of IT enterprises.
texts.text: No information security program has unlimited resources. It is crucial for the information security manger to maximize operational productivity, especially in light of the rapid growth of IT enterprises.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ways productivity can be improved include using automation technologies, outsourcing low-value operational tasks and leveraging the activities of other organizational units. Security management automation technologies can act as workforce multipliers, increasing the accomplishment of operational tasks many times over. Vulnerability scanning tools are an outstanding example of this effect: Manual vulnerability assessment that once took several individuals several weeks can now be accomplished in hours or days. The personnel cost savings can often justify the expense of such tools.

The personnel cost savings can often justify the expense of such tools.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Productivity measures are most useful when employed in a time-based comparison analysis. This approach provides a powerful demonstration of security automation value by showing productivity before and after application of a productivity-boosting technology. Using this approach, the information security manager can demonstrate returns on security investments.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Productivity is a measure of work product generated per resource. For example, if analysis of event log entries is the work product and a security analyst is the resource, the measure of productivity is event log entries analyzed per analyst. Productivity measures can be applied to technology resources in addition to personnel (e.g., network packets processed per IDS node).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Technology purchase and deployment efforts represent only a fraction of full life cycle costs. The information security manager must regularly consider the total costs of maintaining, operating and administering technical security components. In addition, the personnel costs associated with ongoing operational and management activities should be considered. These analyses should be shared with the security steering committee to help identify areas of opportunity for improving costeffectiveness and to assist in forecasting future resource needs.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Even in a tightly controlled technical environment, personnel actions can present threats that can be mitigated only through education and awareness. It is important for the information security program to implement processes for tracking the ongoing effectiveness of awareness programs.
texts.text: Even in a tightly controlled technical environment, personnel actions can present threats that can be mitigated only through education and awareness. It is important for the information security program to implement processes for tracking the ongoing effectiveness of awareness programs.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It is important for the information security program to be financially sustainable because financial constraints are a common reason for security lapses, including failure to plan for ongoing maintenance requirements. The information security manager must work to maximize the value of each security investment to control information security expenses and ensure sustainable achievement of objectives.
texts.text: It is important for the information security program to be financially sustainable because financial constraints are a common reason for security lapses, including failure to plan for ongoing maintenance requirements. The information security manager must work to maximize the value of each security investment to control information security expenses and ensure sustainable achievement of objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This process begins with accurate cost forecasting and budgeting. The success of this activity is generally established by monitoring budget utilization versus original projections and can help identify issues with security cost planning. In addition to measuring budgeting effectiveness, the information security manager should implement procedures to measure the ongoing cost-effectiveness of security components, most often accomplished by tracking cost-result ratios. This approach establishes cost-efficiency goals for new technologies and improvement goals for existing technologies by measuring the total cost of generating a specific result.

Records of initial training, acceptance of policies and usage agreements, and ongoing awareness updates are useful metrics relative to the actual training program. texts.orig: Case Study
texts.text: Case Study

texts.label: text
texts.orig: At the start of a multinational corporation's financial year, a new information security manager was hired to oversee the firm's information security program. The information security manager requested and obtained policies and procedures, prior year internal audits, and results from the most recent external audits.
texts.text: At the start of a multinational corporation's financial year, a new information security manager was hired to oversee the firm's information security program. The information security manager requested and obtained policies and procedures, prior year internal audits, and results from the most recent external audits.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Upon reviewing information provided by internal audit, the information security manager focused on the change management component of the overall information security program. In assessing the control design effectiveness for the change management process, the manager noted, through interviews with key IT personnel, that the firm used a proprietary change control system (dubbed GLASS) to enter change requests and then track them through the change management process taking into account approvals and plans for both rolling out and backing out changes. GLASS keeps a record of all changes made to the billing system, along with the associated date, using unique ideptifiers for each change and audit logs that capture other billing system activities.
texts.text: Upon reviewing information provided by internal audit, the information security manager focused on the change management component of the overall information security program. In assessing the control design effectiveness for the change management process, the manager noted, through interviews with key IT personnel, that the firm used a proprietary change control system (dubbed GLASS) to enter change requests and then track them through the change management process taking into account approvals and plans for both rolling out and backing out changes. GLASS keeps a record of all changes made to the billing system, along with the associated date, using unique ideptifiers for each change and audit logs that capture other billing system activities.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To determine operational effectiveness for the control process, the information security manager conducted interviews with technology owners for the billing system and the firm's audit personnel, then used a random sample of changes taken from the proprietary change control system. The sampling methodology that was used concurred with the firm's internal audit policies. The resulting control assessment involved in the audit was conducted, along the parameters required by the firms' policies and procedures. The change control system passed and no exceptions were found.
texts.text: To determine operational effectiveness for the control process, the information security manager conducted interviews with technology owners for the billing system and the firm's audit personnel, then used a random sample of changes taken from the proprietary change control system. The sampling methodology that was used concurred with the firm's internal audit policies. The resulting control assessment involved in the audit was conducted, along the parameters required by the firms' policies and procedures. The change control system passed and no exceptions were found.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: However, the firm's external audit determined that there were changes to the system that did not have the required approvals. Reviewing the policies and procedures, the information security manager could not find any obvious reason for missing the changes during the internal audit. Through subsequent investigation with the audit team and personnel responsible for migrating changes into one of the production systems, the information security manager determined that GLASS was not the sole point of entry for change requests but could be bypassed.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.1 Incident Management and Incident Response Overview
texts.text: 4.1 Incident Management and Incident Response Overview

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An incident management program is a subset of risk management, with a focus on the planning, preparation and identification of events that deviate from normal, planned operations. The desired goal is to: 1) reduce the impact felt by an enterprise and 2) recover and resume operations at acceptable levels. The speed with which an enterprise can identify, analyze, respond to and recover from an incident reduces the impact felt by the enterprise and ultimately the costs associated with the incident. This normally results in senior management understanding that the enterprise needs an effective and efficient means of responding to an incident.

The desired goal is to: 1) reduce the impact felt by an enterprise and 2) recover and resume operations at acceptable levels. The speed with which an enterprise can identify, analyze, respond to and recover from an incident reduces the impact felt by the enterprise and ultimately the costs associated with the incident. This normally results in senior management understanding that the enterprise needs an effective and efficient means of responding to an incident.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Individual program activities and resources vary based upon an enterprise's maturity, industry, strategic goals, compliance requirements, geographic operations, staffing levels and expressed desire or need to address incidents. Mature enterprises in highly regulated industries may have more capabilities, infrastructure, and resources dedicated to incident management in contrast to enterprises that do not have the same or similar drivers. Each enterprise must decide on the structure and operations that are reasonable and appropriate; there is no one-size-fits-all answer for incident management. What works for one team may not work for another based upon various constraints and operational requirements.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4.1.1 The Relationship Between Incident Management and Incident Response
texts.text: 4.1.1 The Relationship Between Incident Management and Incident Response

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Subtle differences and nuances exist between incident management and incident response functions. Incident management is the ability to provide and ensure the start-to-finish management of an incident within the enterprise. This means identifying how tasks and processes relate to one another, how information is exchanged (internally and externally) and what actions need to be coordinated to successfully manage an incident. Incident response includes the processes, procedures and activities performed when responding to an incident and focuses on the identification, triage, containment, eradication and recovery actions taken to resume normal, planned operations.
texts.text: Subtle differences and nuances exist between incident management and incident response functions. Incident management is the ability to provide and ensure the start-to-finish management of an incident within the enterprise. This means identifying how tasks and processes relate to one another, how information is exchanged (internally and externally) and what actions need to be coordinated to successfully manage an incident. Incident response includes the processes, procedures and activities performed when responding to an incident and focuses on the identification, triage, containment, eradication and recovery actions taken to resume normal, planned operations.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Briefly, incident management includes all the processes, practices and activities that take place prior to, during and after an incident. In contrast, incident response is a subset of activities performed when an incident is declared by the enterprise.
texts.text: Briefly, incident management includes all the processes, practices and activities that take place prior to, during and after an incident. In contrast, incident response is a subset of activities performed when an incident is declared by the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Together, incident management and incident response capabilities are the operationalization of emergency operations in light of an adverse event that impacts an enterprise. Both are components of overall organizational resiliency and risk management. Incident management and response capabilities help to ensure risk to the enterprise is properly managed and addressed. Achieving this aim requires not only acknowledgment by senior management, but also reasonable and appropriate commitments to ensure that risk is sufficiently addressed and efficiently and effectively managed to the acceptable risk tolerance level.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Having an effective incident management capability in place is an important part of the deployment and implementation of any system. Enterprises now realize that active communication and collaboration between the business (e.g. system, risk and control owners), its technical counterparts (e.g., the application developers, system and network administrators, information and cybersecurity) and staff performing and supporting incident management activities provide the best insight for developing approaches to security baselines, better defensive practices, and more streamlined response processes to identify, detect, prevent, respond and recover from the growing variety of threats being faced. At the same time, an effective incident management capability increases overall organizational resiliency efforts in time of need.

texts.orig: By definition, incidents are unexpected events. The ability to detect, identify and assess the situation, determine the causes and quickly arrive at solutions can mean the difference between an inconvenience and a disaster. An important consideration is recognizing the point at which an incident becomes a problem and, subsequently, when the inability to adequately address a problem calls for the declaration of a disaster. The time to make those determinations is not in the middle of a crisis. The progression of a disaster is shown in figure 4.2.

texts.orig: Rigorous planning and commitment of resources are necessary to adequately plan for such events. As with other aspects of security, it is critical to achieve stakeholder consensus and senior management support for an effective incident management capability. Support can be gained as a result of unacceptable impacts of prior incidents to the enterprise or from developing a persuasive business case detailing examples of similar events in other enterprises that show the consequences of inadequate incident management. Incident management and response can lead to lower overall security costs by setting baselines to address common events and providing protection with an adequate response, containment and recovery capability. This is similar to the common approach for protecting against fire by a combination of reasonable preventive controls, coupled with an effective fire detection system, evacuation plans and triggers for fire department response, complemented with insurance policies in the event that incident management and response measures fall short. While a totally fireproof structure could be built, optimal costeffectiveness uses a combination of risk management approaches developed through trial and error.

texts.orig: Severity criteria should be consistent, concisely described and easy to understand so severity levels of similar events are uniformly determined. Escalation and incident declaration criteria must also be established so it is clear who has the authority to determine the response level, activate the teams, declare an incident or disaster and mobilize the appropriate teams to initiate containment and recovery processes. Severity criteria and their use must be widely published and communicated to all relevant parties. Personnel must be trained to recognize potential incidents and provide proper classification, and they must be trained in notification, reporting and escalation requirements. The information security manager must be aware that, regardless of how well incidents are planned for and handled, there is always the possibility that events will escalate to a disaster.

texts.orig: 4.2 Incident Management and Incident Response Plans
texts.text: 4.2 Incident Management and Incident Response Plans

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Effective incident management ensures that incidents are identified, detected, recorded and managed to limit impacts. Recording incidents is required so incident response activities can be tracked, information can be provided to aid planning activities and no aspect of an incident is inadvertently overlooked. Recording is required to properly document information, potentially including forensics data that can be used to pursue disciplinary or legal options. Incidents must be classified to ensure that they are correctly prioritized and routed to the correct resources. Incident management includes initial support processes that allow new incidents to be checked against known errors and problems so that any previously identified workarounds can be quickly identified.

Incidents must be classified to ensure that they are correctly prioritized and routed to the correct resources. Incident management includes initial support processes that allow new incidents to be checked against known errors and problems so that any previously identified workarounds can be quickly identified.

The process ensures that the incidents are owned, tracked and monitored throughout their life cycle. There may be occasions when major incidents require a response above and beyond what is provided through the normal incident process, and they may require activation of C/DR capabilities.

texts.orig: 4.2.5 Incident Management Objectives
texts.text: 4.2.5 Incident Management Objectives

texts.label: text
texts.orig: At its core, incident management exists to address the inevitable events that threaten the operation of any enterprise. It serves as the next-to-last safety net after controls have failed to prevent or contain an incident. The primary purpose is to respond to and contain security incidents and restore normal operations as quickly as possible in the event of an incident. Failing to do so will often result in the declaration of a disaster, and the need for recovery operations. This may include the move to an alternative site to restore operations as defined within the BC/DR plans.

Failing to do so will often result in the declaration of a disaster, and the need for recovery operations. texts.orig: The objectives of incident management are to:
texts.text: The objectives of incident management are to:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Handle incidents when they occur so the exposure can be contained or eradicated to enable recovery within recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs).
texts.text: Handle incidents when they occur so the exposure can be contained or eradicated to enable recovery within recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Restore systems and business processes to normal operation.
texts.text: Restore systems and business processes to normal operation.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Prevent incidents from recurring by documenting and learning from past incidents.
texts.text: Prevent incidents from recurring by documenting and learning from past incidents.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Deploy proactive countermeasures to ● prevent/minimize the probability of incidents occurring in the future.
texts.text: Deploy proactive countermeasures to ● prevent/minimize the probability of incidents occurring in the future.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Deploy safeguards to protect and reduce impact to assets in the event of an incident occurring.
texts.text: Deploy safeguards to protect and reduce impact to assets in the event of an incident occurring.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ideally, incident management and response capabilities must effectively address a wide range of possible unexpected events. Enterprises need to ensure not only that they have well-developed monitoring capabilities for key controls in order to provide early detection of potential problems, but also that these capabilities are accessible to the appropriate incident management personnel. Personnel should be trained in assessing the situation, conducting triage and managing effective responses that maximize operational continuity and minimize impacts. Incident managers will have provisions in place to capture all relevant information and apply previously learned lessons. They will be prepared for a disaster through well-defined criteria, experience, knowledge and authority to invoke the disaster recovery processes necessary to maintain or recover operational status.

texts.orig: Management support—Senior management buy-in is essential for establishing a successful incident management capability within an enterprise. A lack of support can result in a number of issues. For example, the inability to respond to an incident due to existing silos within the enterprise, untrained team members due to underfunding, insufficient budget allocation to allow for effective and efficient response, or to attract or retain qualified personnel. The plan should lay out the necessary resources and management support. The IRP should include the following elements:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The role the information security manager has within BC, DR planning and incident response is going to be influenced by multiple factors, such as the enterprise's size, the industry, applicable regulatory requirements and the maturity of BC, DR and incident response capabilities. The information security manager typically is responsible for responding to information securityrelated incidents.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In smaller enterprises, the information security manager may be involved in all BC, DR and incident response functions—assisting the business units in completing their business impact analyses (BIAs), working with the IT department to identify suitable backup and recovery solutions, coordinating incident response efforts as events are escalated, and delivering normal information security services needed by the enterprise.
texts.text: In smaller enterprises, the information security manager may be involved in all BC, DR and incident response functions—assisting the business units in completing their business impact analyses (BIAs), working with the IT department to identify suitable backup and recovery solutions, coordinating incident response efforts as events are escalated, and delivering normal information security services needed by the enterprise.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In larger enterprises, BC, DR and incident response business functions may be separate departments, each with their own dedicated staff and budgets needed to support operations. Here, the role of the information security manager may be an internal consultant, advising as a subject matter expert in any of the related functions. The information security manager may be a general contributor—supporting and augmenting existing operations and delivering services in support of business need—or may function purely as a business peer, with security incidents being reported for the purposes of monitoring, prioritization and remediation, and with response efforts performed by the incident response department.

Here, the role of the information security manager may be an internal consultant, advising as a subject matter expert in any of the related functions. The information security manager may be a general contributor—supporting and augmenting existing operations and delivering services in support of business need—or may function purely as a business peer, with security incidents being reported for the purposes of monitoring, prioritization and remediation, and with response efforts performed by the incident response department.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Regardless of the environment the information security manager is operating in, it is important to have a good conceptual and practical understanding of what is required to adequately address related responsibilities. In addition, there must be a good understanding of the BC and DR processes. This is to ensure that incident management and response plans and activities integrate well with the overall BCP and DRP in the event that an incident escalates to a disaster.

Any risk that materializes and is not prevented by the enterprise's internal controls constitutes an incident that must be managed and responded to with the intent that it does not escalate into a disaster.

An effective outcome is a set of plans that define which departments are involved in various incident management and response activities and specify that those linkages have been tested under realistic conditions.

texts.orig: 4.2.12 Resource Management
texts.text: 4.2.12 Resource Management

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Resource management encompasses time, people, budget and other factors to achieve objectives efficiently under given resource constraints. Incident management and response activities consume resources that must be managed to achieve optimal effectiveness. This is accomplished by ensuring appropriate oversight, monitoring of resources and regular reporting. When it is not possible to achieve all objectives, effective resource management ensures that the most important priorities are addressed first. In terms of incident response, effective triage capabilities ensure that limited resources are applied most effectively to contain and limit damage. This is based on quickly identifying compromised assets that cannot be quickly addressed, the assets that are unaffected and can wait, and the ones that can most efficiently be restored with the available resources.

Triage—Triage is a process of sorting, categorizing, correlating, prioritizing and assigning incoming reports/events into (typically three) categories: the problems that cannot be readily resolved, those that can wait and those that can be efficiently addressed with the resources available. It is an essential element of any incident management capability to ensure maximum effectiveness of limited resources. It can also serve as a single point of entry for any IMT communication and information.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Most enterprises have some sort of ad hoc or formal incident response capability. The information security manager must identify what is already in place as a basis for understanding the current state. There are many ways to do this, including:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Survey of senior management, business managers and IT representatives—Uses input from senior management, business line managers and technology representatives, employee surveys and focus groups to gather information to help determine the past performance and perception of the IMT and its process capabilities.

This is the easiest method because it does not require participation from many stakeholders. The disadvantage of this method is that it may provide only a limited view of current capabilities and other aspects that stakeholders may consider important.

texts.orig: Vulnerabilities
texts.text: Vulnerabilities

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A weakness in a system, technology, process, person or control that can be exploited and result in compromise is a vulnerability. A vulnerability that can be exploited by threats results in risk. One aspect of risk management is managing vulnerabilities to maintain risk within acceptable limits as determined by the enterprise's risk appetite and tolerance criteria. Vulnerability management is part of the incident management capability; it is the proactive identification, monitoring and repair of any weaknesses.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The IRP is the operational component of incident management. The plan details the actions, personnel and activities that take place in case adverse events result in the loss of data, information systems or processes. The plan should include the formation, management and maintenance of the incident response team.

texts.text: 4.2.17 Incident Management and Response Teams

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The plan must identify teams and define their assigned responsibilities ahead of an incident occurring. To implement the strategies that have been developed for business recovery, key decision-making, technical and end-user team leaders need to be designated and trained. Depending on the size of the business operation, the team may consist of a single person. The involvement of these teams depends on the level of the disruption of service and the types of assets lost, compromised, damaged or endangered. A matrix should be developed that indicates the correlations among the functions of the different teams. This will facilitate estimating the magnitude of the effort and activating the appropriate combination of teams. Examples of the kinds of teams usually needed include:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Training the response teams is not only essential but also critical. The information security manager should develop reasonable, real-world event scenarios and test the response and recovery plans to ensure that team participants are familiar with their tasks and responsibilities. Through this process, the teams will identify the resources they require for response and recovery. An added value of training is detecting and modifying ambiguous procedures to achieve clarity and determining recovery resources that may not be adequate or effective.

The information security manager should understand how obtaining timely and relevant information can help the enterprise respond quickly and efficiently and will ultimately limit the potential loss and damage that may occur as the result of an incident. Notification mechanisms that enable an automated detection system or monitor to send email or phone messages should be used whenever possible. The following functions are most likely to need information concerning incidents when they occur:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When developing and maintaining an incident management plan, there may be unanticipated challenges as the result of:
texts.text: When developing and maintaining an incident management plan, there may be unanticipated challenges as the result of:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Lack of management buy-in and organizational consensus—Most challenges result from a lack of management buy-in and consensus among the business units. When an incident occurs, the management response may not be provided as expected, thus hindering incident management efforts. This may happen when senior management and other stakeholders or constituents are not involved in incident management planning and implementation. Challenges can also result from the lack of regular meetings between the IMT and constituents. A sense of ownership among constituents in incident management helps to ensure that sufficient resources and support are available for the IMT.
texts.text: Lack of management buy-in and organizational consensus—Most challenges result from a lack of management buy-in and consensus among the business units. When an incident occurs, the management response may not be provided as expected, thus hindering incident management efforts. This may happen when senior management and other stakeholders or constituents are not involved in incident management planning and implementation. Challenges can also result from the lack of regular meetings between the IMT and constituents. A sense of ownership among constituents in incident management helps to ensure that sufficient resources and support are available for the IMT.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: ● Mismatch to organizational goals and structure—Business operates at an accelerated rate and may change significantly over a short period of time. Incident management may not be able to cope with the speed or nature of changes happening within the enterprise. Consider a situation in which the business expands to emerging countries. The presence in new countries may grow at a significant rate; however, it may be difficult to expand incident management capabilities. A round of discussions may be needed to identify critical business functions and local stakeholders and understand local regulations. Senior management is usually occupied with business matters at this stage and may not be able to invest time in incident management. It is the responsibility of the IMT to identify any critical issues and make them known to executive management.

The lack of a champion is likely to reduce the focus and resources devoted to implementing the plan.

texts.orig: Loss of confidentiality—In this context, confidentiality refers to the protection of information from unauthorized disclosure. The impact of unauthorized disclosure of confidential information can range from the jeopardizing of national security to the disclosure of private consumer data. Unauthorized, unanticipated or unintentional disclosure of private consumer or other regulated data can result in loss of public confidence, loss of customer base and legal action against the enterprise.
texts.text: Loss of confidentiality—In this context, confidentiality refers to the protection of information from unauthorized disclosure. The impact of unauthorized disclosure of confidential information can range from the jeopardizing of national security to the disclosure of private consumer data. Unauthorized, unanticipated or unintentional disclosure of private consumer or other regulated data can result in loss of public confidence, loss of customer base and legal action against the enterprise.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Loss of integrity—System and data integrity refers to the requirement that information be protected from improper modification. Integrity is lost if unauthorized or erroneous changes are made to the data or IT system by either intentional or accidental acts. If the loss of system or data integrity is not corrected, continued use of the contaminated system or corrupted data could result in broader corruption, fraud or misinformed decisions. Also, violation of integrity may be the first step in a successful attack against system availability or confidentiality.

Also, violation of integrity may be the first step in a successful attack against system availability or confidentiality.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Loss of availability—If a mission-critical IT system or process is unavailable to its end users, the enterprise's mission may be affected. Loss of system functionality and operational effectiveness, for example, may result in loss of productive time, thus impeding the end users' performance of their functions in supporting the enterprise's mission.
texts.text: Loss of availability—If a mission-critical IT system or process is unavailable to its end users, the enterprise's mission may be affected. Loss of system functionality and operational effectiveness, for example, may result in loss of productive time, thus impeding the end users' performance of their functions in supporting the enterprise's mission.

texts.orig: In conducting an impact analysis, consideration should be given to the advantages and disadvantages of quantitative versus qualitative assessments. The main advantage of the qualitative impact analysis is that it prioritizes the risk and identifies areas for immediate improvement in addressing the vulnerabilities. The disadvantage of the qualitative analysis is that it does not provide specific quantifiable measurements of the magnitude of the impacts, therefore making a costbenefit analysis of any recommended controls difficult.

texts.orig: Another way of viewing a BIA is that it is a business function designed to identify the resources that are most important to an enterprise and the impact resulting from disruption or availability loss. It should also result in an understanding of process flows in the enterprise needed to optimize recovery priorities based on system dependencies and interdependencies. When conducted properly, a BIA facilitates understanding the amount of potential loss (and various other unwanted effects) that could occur from certain types of events. Potential loss includes direct financial loss and less tangible types of loss, such as reputational damage or failure to achieve regulatory compliance.

texts.orig: Despite the high level of importance of understanding the business impact of incidents on the business process, many enterprises fail to undertake this assessment. Another common problem is the failure to update BIAs when systems and business functions are added or changed. A BIA is a part of risk assessment insofar as the degree of risk exposure will correlate to the potential for an event resulting in an impact. The BIA is also used to determine the consequences, whereas the risk determination calculates both the probability and consequences.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Effective integration of incident response and BC/DR planning requires the relationships among RTO, RPO, SDO and MTO to be carefully considered as the transition from incident response to disaster recovery operations for any solutions aside from mirrored or duplicate processing sites will require time. This is important to consider as RTOs, MTOs and AIWs are directly influenced by recovery capabilities and the failure to plan accordingly often results in the inability to achieve target objectives.
texts.text: Effective integration of incident response and BC/DR planning requires the relationships among RTO, RPO, SDO and MTO to be carefully considered as the transition from incident response to disaster recovery operations for any solutions aside from mirrored or duplicate processing sites will require time. This is important to consider as RTOs, MTOs and AIWs are directly influenced by recovery capabilities and the failure to plan accordingly often results in the inability to achieve target objectives.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: DR historically comprises the plan to recover an ITprocessing facility or the plan by business units to recover an operational facility. With the continued growth and widespread adoption of cloud services, there is a movement away from thinking of IT in terms of facilities toward viewing IT as a capability. The incident management and recovery plan must be consistent with and support the overall IT plan of the enterprise. BC planning, DR and incident response do not necessarily have to be combined into a single plan; however, each must be consistent with the other and integrated so that the transition to declaration of a disaster is effective.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Alternative routing—Alternative routing means routing information via an alternative medium such as copper cable or fiber optics. This involves use of different networks, circuits or end points, if the normal network is unavailable. Most local carriers are deploying counter-rotating fiber-optic rings. These rings have fiber-optic cables that transmit information in two directions and in separate cable sheaths for increased protection. Currently, these rings connect through one central switching office. However, future expansion of the rings may incorporate a second central office in the circuit. Some carriers are offering alternative routes to different points of presence or alternative central offices. Other examples include dial-up circuits as an alternative to dedicated circuits, a cellular phone and microwave communications as alternatives to land circuits and couriers as alternatives to electronic transmissions.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Diverse routing—This is the method of routing traffic through split cable facilities or duplicate cable facilities. This can be accomplished with different or duplicate cable sheaths. If different cable sheaths are used, the cable may be in the same conduit and therefore subject to the same interruptions as the cable it is backing up. The communication service subscriber can duplicate the facilities by having alternative routes, although the entrance to and from the customer's premises may be in the same conduit. The subscriber can obtain diverse routing and alternative routing from the local carrier, including dual entrance facilities; however, acquiring this type of access is time-consuming and costly. Most carriers provide facilities for alternative and diverse routing, although most services are transmitted over terrestrial media. These cable facilities are usually located in the ground or the basement of buildings that house computer equipment. Ground-based facilities are at risk due to the aging infrastructures of cities. In addition, cable-based facilities usually share space with mechanical and electrical systems

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Telephony recovery—With the increased use of network based Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP)- based telephony, careful attention and consideration needs to be given to business functions that require high availability and accessibility to telephony services. This is especially true if the enterprise is in a time-sensitive industry or provides critical services, such as healthcare or emergency services. While it may appear cost-effective to reduce and consolidate the number of providers to provide both network and telephony over the provider's data circuits, this carries the risk of creating a single point of failure. Information security managers should advise proper diversification of carriers and use of plain old telephone service (POTS) lines to reduce the impact and chances associated with a total communication failure if the data services should be interrupted.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The loss or disruption of servers managing sensitive and critical business processes could have catastrophic effects on an enterprise. Plans should include operational failover methods to prevent servers from going offline for an extended period of time. Server recovery should be included in the DRP. Some techniques for providing failover or fault-tolerant capabilities include the use of universal power supplies (UPSs) and failover systems to prevent power failures of varying levels.

Plans should include operational failover methods to prevent servers from going offline for an extended period of time. Server recovery should be included in the DRP. Some techniques for providing failover or fault-tolerant capabilities include the use of universal power supplies (UPSs) and failover systems to prevent power failures of varying levels.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Direct attached storage (DAS) is a data storage and availability solution in which the storage device (e.g., disk drive) is directly attached to a server or client. In order for multiple users to access the DAS, each needs to have direct access to the server that is housing the storage device. If the need for more storage arises, the server or client needs to be taken offline so additional drives can be installed, which affects availability.
texts.text: Direct attached storage (DAS) is a data storage and availability solution in which the storage device (e.g., disk drive) is directly attached to a server or client. In order for multiple users to access the DAS, each needs to have direct access to the server that is housing the storage device. If the need for more storage arises, the server or client needs to be taken offline so additional drives can be installed, which affects availability.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Network attached storage (NAS) is a dedicated network attached data storage appliance with its own operating system (e.g., TrueNAS). File storage and user accessibility are provided through an existing Ethernet network. Adding storage to the NAS causes minimal downtime, because the connection is to the network rather than the server; therefore, availability is not necessarily impacted as storage needs increase. Connectivity and access to files are typically facilitated through a variety of protocols such as Network File Share or Server Message Block. The ability to access files via a web browser, dedicated application or command line tools may also be available in NAS appliances.

File storage and user accessibility are provided through an existing Ethernet network. Adding storage to the NAS causes minimal downtime, because the connection is to the network rather than the server; therefore, availability is not necessarily impacted as storage needs increase. Connectivity and access to files are typically facilitated through a variety of protocols such as Network File Share or Server Message Block. The ability to access files via a web browser, dedicated application or command line tools may also be available in NAS appliances.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A storage area network (SAN) is a high-speed, specialpurpose network that provides mass storage using remote interconnected devices——such as disk arrays, tape libraries or optical jukeboxes—with associated data servers that function as if they were attached locally. SANs are typically part of the overall network of computing resources for larger enterprises but may also serve as remote resources for backup and archival storage. SANs typically support disk mirroring, backup and restore functions, data migration between storage devices, and the sharing of data among different servers in one or more networks.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If the RTO is instantaneous and the RPO is equally stringent (i.e., the goal is for users to experience no downtime), then a fault-tolerant storage solution is established. Fault-tolerant servers provide for fail-safe redundancy through mirrored images of the primary server. Using this approach also entails distributed processing of a server load—a concept referred to as load balancing or clustering—where all servers take part in processing. In this arrangement, an intelligent cluster unit provides for load balancing for improved performance. This type of server architecture is transparent to users. The only thing that may be noticeable to a user is performance degradation if a server fails.

Fault-tolerant servers provide for fail-safe redundancy through mirrored images of the primary server. Using this approach also entails distributed processing of a server load—a concept referred to as load balancing or clustering—where all servers take part in processing. In this arrangement, an intelligent cluster unit provides for load balancing for improved performance. This type of server architecture is transparent to users. The only thing that may be noticeable to a user is performance degradation if a server fails.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The information security manager must be aware of the costs associated with fault-tolerant solutions and difficulties in achieving this state of data availability. For example, in a virtual environment, multiple instances (copies) of a virtual machine (VM) running in parallel must exist. Any change in the state of the primary VM (such as modification of a file) must be applied on all the secondary VMs in real time.

For example, in a virtual environment, multiple instances (copies) of a virtual machine (VM) running in parallel must exist. Any change in the state of the primary VM (such as modification of a file) must be applied on all the secondary VMs in real time.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If the RTO and RPO are more flexible (i.e., the business will tolerate a limited amount of downtime), then a highavailability storage solution is established. An example of high availability is a set of servers that have a failover relationship. When an application is running and the primary server fails, the application is restarted in the failover server. In this arrangement, the most current work in progress may be lost; however, the application could be up and running within seconds. High availability solutions are less costly to implement than those designed for 100 percent fault tolerance. See figure 4.6.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The IRP should include information regarding the enterprise's insurance plans, including general coverage, cyber insurance or IT-related insurance. Some elements of the enterprise's coverage, such as a business interruption policy, may provide some level of protection and should be considered as part of the plan. Current information systems processing insurance policies usually require a multi-peril policy designed to provide various types of IT coverage. These policies should be constructed modularly, so they can be adapted to the insured's particular IT environment.

Some elements of the enterprise's coverage, such as a business interruption policy, may provide some level of protection and should be considered as part of the plan. Current information systems processing insurance policies usually require a multi-peril policy designed to provide various types of IT coverage. These policies should be constructed modularly, so they can be adapted to the insured's particular IT environment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: An enterprise typically cannot insure against failure to comply with legal and regulatory requirements or any other breach of the law. There are usually a number of other exclusions and deductibles, and careful review by the information security manager is required to gain a clear understanding of the actual protection provided.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: IT equipment and facilities—Coverage of physical damage to the information processing facility (IPF) and owned equipment. An enterprise should also insure leased equipment if it is obtained when the lessee is responsible for hazard coverage. The information security manager should review these policies carefully; many policies are worded so that insurers are obligated to replace damaged or destroyed equipment with like kind and quality, not necessarily the identical brand and model.

texts.orig: Media (software) reconstruction—Covers damage to computer-related media that are the property of the insured and for which the insured may be liable. Insurance is available for on-premises, off-premises or in-transit disasters and covers the actual reproduction cost of the property. Considerations in determining the amount of coverage needed are programming costs to reproduce the media damaged, backup expenses, and physical replacement of media devices such as tapes, cartridges and disks.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There are several considerations when developing response and recovery plans, including available resources; expected services; and the types, kinds and severity of threats faced by the enterprise. The state of monitoring and detection capabilities must be known, and the level of risk the enterprise is willing to accept must be determined, as discussed in Section 2.4.1 Determining Risk Capacity and Acceptable Risk (Risk Appetite). An effective strategy for recovery plans strikes the most cost-effective balance among risk management efforts, incident management and response and BC/DR planning.

texts.orig: The International Consortium for Organizational Resilience30 defines business continuity as "a management process that identifies potential threats to an organization and the impacts to business operations if those threats are realized." Therefore, the relationship between BC and DR is such that the DRP is a subset of the BCP. Specifically, while BCP goals include incident prevention and mitigation, the DRP is focused on what must be done to restore operations after an incident has already taken place. A BCP may be seen as a continuous process that is actively implemented in business-as-usual scenarios, while the DRP is reactive in nature and is implemented only upon satisfaction of a specific set of conditions (i.e., the business has incurred an incident).
